runs.answer: In the preload script, use contextBridge.exposeInMainWorld to expose one small wrapper function per IPC message. The wrapper calls ipcRenderer.invoke('<channel>') and returns its result, e.g. contextBridge.exposeInMainWorld('myAPI', { loadPreferences: () => ipcRenderer.invoke('load-prefs') }). On the main side, the process listens on that channel with ipcMain.handle(). The docs warn against exposing ipcRenderer.send or the whole ipcRenderer.invoke API, because then any website could send arbitrary IPC messages. Even with contextIsolation and contextBridge, give the renderer as little access to Electron APIs as possible.

runs.answer: Use the two-way renderer-to-main pattern: pair `ipcRenderer.invoke` with `ipcMain.handle`. In the main process, register a handler such as `ipcMain.handle('dialog:openFile', handleFileOpen)`. The handler's return value goes back to the original `invoke` call as a Promise. In the preload script, use `contextBridge.exposeInMainWorld('electronAPI', { openFile: () => ipcRenderer.invoke('dialog:openFile') })` to expose one narrow function, not the whole `ipcRenderer.invoke` API, for security reasons. The page then calls `const result = await window.electronAPI.openFile()`. The docs advise against the older `ipcRenderer.send`/`event.reply` and `ipcRenderer.sendSync` approaches, which are kept for historical reasons only; also, an error thrown in a `handle` handler reaches the renderer with only its `message` property.

Use the main-process `globalShortcut` module. Call `globalShortcut.register(accelerator, callback)`, for example with `'CommandOrControl+Alt+R'`. This registers the shortcut with the operating system, so the callback fires even when your app does not have keyboard focus. The module cannot be used before the app's `ready` event, so register inside `app.whenReady()`, and remove shortcuts with `globalShortcut.unregister()` or `unregisterAll()`, for example on `will-quit`. `register()` returns a boolean, and it fails silently if another app already holds that accelerator; you can check with `isRegistered()`. There are platform caveats. On Linux Wayland, binding goes through the `org.freedesktop.portal.GlobalShortcuts` portal: the app needs a valid `desktopName` (or `app.setDesktopName()`), GNOME asks the user for consent, and the real result arrives later in the `registration-resolved` event rather than in the return value. On macOS, a long-standing bug stops it from working with keyboard layouts other than QWERTY.

runs.answer: Use the main-process `globalShortcut` module. Inside `app.whenReady()`, because the module can't be used before the app's `ready` event, call `globalShortcut.register('CommandOrControl+Alt+R', callback)`. This registers the accelerator with the operating system, so the callback fires even when your app is out of focus. A menu-item `accelerator` is different: it only fires while the app is focused. `register()` returns a boolean and fails silently (returns false) if another app already owns that accelerator; you can check with `globalShortcut.isRegistered()`, and you should clean up with `globalShortcut.unregister()` or `unregisterAll()`, for example in `app.on('will-quit')`. Caveats: on Linux Wayland, binding goes through the `org.freedesktop.portal.GlobalShortcuts` portal. That needs a valid reverse-DNS `desktopName` (or `app.setDesktopName()`) matching your .desktop file, may show a consent dialog on GNOME, and reports the real result through the `registration-resolved` event. On macOS, a long-standing bug stops `globalShortcut` from working with non-QWERTY keyboard layouts.

Set `titleBarStyle: 'hidden'` in the `BrowserWindow` constructor to remove the default title bar; on macOS this keeps the traffic-light controls in the upper-left corner. On Windows and Linux, also set `titleBarOverlay: true` to bring back the native minimize, maximize and close buttons. You can instead pass an object with `color`, `symbolColor` and `height` to style them, and `titleBarOverlay` needs a `titleBarStyle` other than `default`. Once the default title bar is gone the window can't be moved, so add the CSS `app-region: drag` to your custom HTML title bar to make it the drag region. The native buttons can sit on the left, the right or both sides, so keep your title bar content inside the safe area given by `env(titlebar-area-x, 0px)` and `env(titlebar-area-width, 100%)` so it doesn't overlap them.

runs.answer: Before the app's `ready` event, call `protocol.registerSchemesAsPrivileged([{ scheme: 'app', privileges: { standard: true, secure: true, supportFetchAPI: true } }])`. You can only call it once. Registering the scheme as `standard` makes relative URLs resolve and turns on web storage (localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB, cookies) and the FileSystem API; all of these are disabled for non-standard schemes. `supportFetchAPI` turns on fetch. After `app.whenReady()`, when the scheme only serves the app's own bundled files, the docs recommend the experimental `protocol.registerSource('app', { routes: [{ match: { host: 'bundle' }, source: { type: 'directory', root: path.join(app.getAppPath(), 'dist') } }] })`: it streams files from disk, including from asar, sets Content-Type from the file extension, serves the route's `index` file for paths ending in `/`, and returns `net::ERR_FILE_NOT_FOUND` for paths outside `root`, all without touching the main thread. The other option is `protocol.handle('app', handler)` returning `net.fetch(pathToFileURL(resolvedPath).toString())`, but then your handler must reject paths that escape the bundle directory itself (for example `app://bundle/../../secret_file.txt`).

runs.answer: Before the app's `ready` event, call `protocol.registerSchemesAsPrivileged([{ scheme: 'app', privileges: { standard: true, secure: true, supportFetchAPI: true } }])`. You can only call it once. `standard: true` is the key setting: without it, a custom scheme behaves like `file://` but cannot resolve relative URLs, the FileSystem API throws security errors, and web storage (localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB, cookies) is turned off. `supportFetchAPI` turns on fetch. After `ready`, serve the bundle with `protocol.handle('app', req => ...)`; the docs' example maps `app://bundle/<path>` to files under `__dirname` with `net.fetch(pathToFileURL(...))` and returns a 400 for paths that escape the bundle, such as `app://bundle/../../secret_file.txt`. Or use the experimental `protocol.registerSource('app', { routes: [{ match: { host: 'bundle' }, source: { type: 'directory', root: path.join(app.getAppPath(), 'dist') } }] })`, which the docs recommend when a scheme only serves the app's own bundled files: it needs no JS handler and runs off the main thread, and it also reads from asar, sets Content-Type from the file extension and serves the route's `index` file for paths ending in `/`. If the window uses a custom `partition` or `session`, register the handler on that session (`ses.protocol.handle`), and note that security checklist item #18 recommends this approach over `file://`.

runs.answer: Use Electron's `utilityProcess` API instead of Node's `child_process.fork`. The Process Model guide says a utility process runs in a full Node.js environment, is meant for work like CPU-intensive tasks that would otherwise run in the main process, and should be preferred over `child_process.fork` whenever you fork a child from main. In the main process, call `utilityProcess.fork(modulePath[, args][, options])`, but only after the app's `ready` event; it returns a `UtilityProcess` EventEmitter. Send it work with `child.postMessage(message, [transfer])`, which can also hand over `MessagePortMain` objects (for example from `new MessageChannelMain()`), and get results back with `child.on('message', ...)`. In the child script, listen with `process.parentPort.once/on('message', (e) => ...)` (transferred ports arrive in `e.ports`) and reply with `process.parentPort.postMessage()`, which fires the 'message' event in main. Manage the process with the 'spawn', 'exit' and 'error' events and `child.kill()`; the guide also says a utility process can talk to a renderer directly over `MessagePort`s.

runs.answer: The docs say to use Electron's `utilityProcess` API. From the main process, call `utilityProcess.fork(modulePath[, args][, options])`, which you can only do after the app's `ready` event. It spawns a child process with full Node.js, works like Node's `child_process.fork`, and the process-model tutorial names CPU-intensive tasks as a use for it and says to prefer it over `child_process.fork`. Main sends work with `child.postMessage(message, [transfer])`, which can also hand over `MessagePortMain` objects, and gets replies through `child.on('message', ...)`. In the child script, `process.parentPort.on('message', (e) => ...)` receives the data as `e.data` and any ports as `e.ports`, and `process.parentPort.postMessage(...)` replies; messages wait in a queue until a handler is registered. The child also has `spawn`/`exit`/`error` events, `child.kill()` and `child.pid`, but the performance guide says to try worker threads or moving the work to a BrowserWindow first and to spawn a dedicated process only "as a last resort".

runs.answer: Call `crashReporter.start({ submitURL: 'https://your-server/submit', uploadToServer: true, globalExtra: {...} })` in the main process as early as possible, ideally before `app.whenReady()`. Electron uses Crashpad: `start()` launches a separate crash handler process, which writes a minidump when the main process crashes or when a child process (renderer, GPU, utility or Node.js child) crashes. Only child processes created after `start()` are monitored, and renderers can't start the reporter; in a renderer, `crashReporter` only offers `addExtraParameter()`, `removeExtraParameter()` and `getParameters()`, called from the preload script. When uploads are on, the handler POSTs each report to `submitURL` as gzip-compressed `multipart/form-data` by default. The minidump is in `upload_file_minidump`, alongside fields such as `process_type` (`browser` for the main process, `renderer`), `ver`, `_productName`, `_version`, `guid`, `platform`, and your `globalExtra` and per-process values. Your server should respond with 200, and the response body is stored as the report ID that `getUploadedReports()` returns; any server that accepts Breakpad or Crashpad minidumps works. To ask for consent first, start with `uploadToServer: false` and call `crashReporter.setUploadToServer(true)` when the user opts in (reports from before that are never sent), and test the setup with `process.crash()`; the crash reporter does nothing in Mac App Store builds.

runs.answer: Call `crashReporter.start({ submitURL: 'https://your-server/submit', uploadToServer: true, globalExtra: {...} })` once in the main process, as early as possible and ideally before `app.whenReady()`. Electron then starts a separate Crashpad handler process. It writes minidumps for main-process crashes and automatically monitors renderers and other child processes created after `start()`. Processes started before that call are not monitored. Each crash is uploaded to `submitURL` as a gzip-compressed `multipart/form-data` POST using the Breakpad upload protocol, so any server that accepts Breakpad or Crashpad dumps will work. The dump arrives in `upload_file_minidump`, along with fields such as `process_type` (`browser` for main, `renderer`), `ver`, `_productName`, `_version`, `guid`, `platform` and your `globalExtra` and per-process annotations; your server should reply 200, and the response body becomes the report ID that `getUploadedReports()` returns. Renderers cannot start the reporter, but their preload script can add annotations with `crashReporter.addExtraParameter()` (through `contextBridge` when context isolation is on). Dumps are also written under `app.getPath('crashDumps')`, and to ask for consent you can start with `uploadToServer: false` and call `crashReporter.setUploadToServer(true)` when the user opts in (dumps from before that are never sent). You can test the setup with `process.crash()`; in Mac App Store builds the reporter does nothing.

runs.answer: Use Electron's offscreen rendering. Create a `BrowserWindow` with `webPreferences: { offscreen: true }` and load the page. The window's content then comes to you as a bitmap or GPU texture instead of being shown, and an offscreen window is always frameless. Listen to `win.webContents.on('paint', (event, dirtyRect, image) => …)`, which fires each time a new frame is generated. `image` is a `NativeImage` of the whole frame (for example `image.toBitmap()` or `image.toPNG()`), and `dirtyRect` marks the changed area in `toBitmap()` pixels. Set the rate with `webContents.setFrameRate()` (at most 240 when `useSharedTexture` is false) and pause or resume with `stopPainting()`/`startPainting()`; when nothing on the page changes, no frames are generated. Calling `app.disableHardwareAcceleration()` picks the faster software (CPU) mode; the default GPU mode copies each frame into a CPU bitmap, which is slower but supports WebGL and 3D CSS. `offscreen: { useSharedTexture: true }` instead delivers GPU textures on `event.texture`; this is experimental, needs a native module, and each texture must be `release()`d.

runs.answer: Use Electron's offscreen rendering (OSR), which the glossary says lets you render a page without showing it on screen: create a BrowserWindow with `webPreferences: { offscreen: true }` and load your page. Each new frame fires the `webContents` 'paint' event with `(event, dirtyRect, image)`, where `image` is a NativeImage of the whole frame (for example `image.toBitmap()` or `image.toPNG()`). Only the dirty area is passed, and no frames are produced while nothing on the page changes. `contents.invalidate()` forces a full repaint and a new 'paint' event. Set the frame rate with `webContents.setFrameRate(fps)` (1–240 in bitmap mode) and control capture with `startPainting()`/`stopPainting()`. For the fastest CPU bitmaps, call `app.disableHardwareAcceleration()` to use the software output device. The default GPU mode copies each frame from GPU to CPU but supports WebGL and 3D CSS, and `offscreen.useSharedTexture: true` gives GPU textures instead of bitmaps.

runs.answer: Calling `app.quit()` (or pressing Cmd+Q) emits `before-quit` first, before any window starts closing. Electron then tries to close every window, and a window's `beforeunload` handler can cancel the quit by returning `false`. Only if all windows close does it emit `will-quit`, and then `quit` (with an `exitCode`) as the app exits; `window-all-closed` is not emitted on this path. There are two exceptions: after `autoUpdater.quitAndInstall()`, `before-quit` fires only once all windows have emitted `close` and closed, and on Windows none of these events fire when the system shuts down or restarts or the user logs out. To postpone quitting, call `event.preventDefault()` in `before-quit` or `will-quit`; `quit` has no such option. The docs show the async version in `will-quit`: return early if nothing is pending, otherwise call `event.preventDefault()` and start the async write, then in its `.finally()` clear the pending flag and call `app.quit()` again, so the second pass goes through.

A window can also cancel the quit from its `close` event (preventDefault) or `beforeunload` (returnValue = false), and on Windows `before-quit`/`will-quit`/`quit` are not emitted when the app closes because of a system shutdown, restart or logout.

runs.answer: Yes. Since electron@28.0.0 the main process uses Node.js's ESM loader, and a file is treated as ESM when it ends in `.mjs` or its nearest parent package.json sets `"type": "module"`. The main caveat is that ES modules load asynchronously, so only side effects of the entry point's static imports run before the app's `ready` event. You must top-level `await` anything that has to finish before `ready` (for example `app.setPath`), especially dynamic `import()` calls. Also, transpilers such as Babel or TypeScript used to turn `import` into synchronous `require` calls, so moving to native ESM can change when code runs. For preloads: ESM preloads must use the `.mjs` extension because preloads ignore `"type": "module"`; sandboxed preloads can't use ESM imports at all (bundle them and keep `require('electron')`); unsandboxed ESM preloads don't block page load when the response body is completely empty (Content-Length: 0), which can cause race conditions (put something like `<html></html>` in the body or switch back to a `.js`/`.cjs` preload); and a preload can only dynamically `import()` Node modules if `contextIsolation` is enabled.

runs.answer: Cookies, cache and other browsing data belong to a session (`ses.cookies` is that session's cookie store). Every window uses the app's default session unless its `webPreferences` sets `partition` or passes a `Session` object as `session`, and `session` wins if both are given. Pages with the same partition string share one session, and a different partition gives a separate one, because `session.fromPartition` returns the existing session for that partition or creates a new one. A partition that starts with `persist:` gives a persistent session that all pages in the app with that partition share; without the prefix the session is in-memory only, and an empty partition means the default session. So to keep separate logins that survive restarts, give each account's window its own `persist:<account>` partition; options such as `cache` can only be set the first time a partition is used.

runs.answer: Cookies and storage belong to a Session, not to a window: unless you set `webPreferences.session` or `webPreferences.partition`, every window uses the app's default session, so all windows share it. To keep accounts apart, give each window its own partition string (or pass a Session object; `session` wins if both are set). Pages with the same partition share one session, and each new partition string gets a new Session instance with its own `ses.cookies`. A partition that starts with `persist:` (for example `session.fromPartition('persist:account1')`) is a persistent session available to every page in the app with that partition, while one without the prefix is an in-memory, temporary session. A BrowserWindow's default session is also persistent, and `ses.storagePath` / `ses.getStoragePath()` gives the folder where a session's data is saved on disk (`null` for in-memory sessions).

Electron's security guide says never to load and run remote code with Node.js integration enabled. Any BrowserWindow, WebContentsView or <webview> that shows remote content should keep `nodeIntegration` off (and not set `nodeIntegrationInWorker`), which has been the default since 5.0.0. The guide suggests showing such content in a `<webview>` or `WebContentsView` with `nodeIntegration` disabled and `contextIsolation` enabled. Context isolation (default since 12.0.0) is still required when `nodeIntegration` is false, because only then is Node truly blocked. The process sandbox (default since 20.0.0, and can be enforced app-wide) should be on in every renderer, because turning off context isolation also turns off the sandbox, and untrusted content should never run in an unsandboxed process. If the site needs extra abilities, give it only what it needs through a preload script that exposes a small API via `contextBridge`. The rest of the checklist says to only load secure content, use `ses.setPermissionRequestHandler()` in sessions that load remote content, keep `webSecurity` on, set a restrictive Content-Security-Policy, leave `allowRunningInsecureContent`, experimental features and `enableBlinkFeatures` off, and disable or limit navigation and new-window creation.

runs.answer: Electron's performance guide says to profile first (Chrome DevTools, Chrome Tracing) to find the real bottleneck. Its checklist then says to check a module's dependencies and `require()` cost before adding it (`node --cpu-prof --heap-prof -e "require('x')"`). Defer expensive setup and load large modules "just in time" instead of at launch, and bundle your code into one file (Webpack, Parcel or rollup) so the `require()` cost is paid only once. Avoid unneeded polyfills and network requests for files you could ship with the app, and call `Menu.setApplicationMenu(null)` before `app.on("ready")` if you don't need the default menu. The main process holds the UI thread, so never run long tasks there: move CPU-heavy work to worker threads or the BrowserWindow (a separate process only as a last resort), avoid sync IPC and `@electron/remote`, and use the async versions of `fs` and `child_process` (in renderers, use `requestIdleCallback()` for small tasks and Web Workers for long ones).

Then avoid the common pitfalls. Check how big a module and its dependencies are, and what `require()` costs, before adding it. Don't load and run code too soon: put off expensive setup work and the `require()` of large modules until they're actually needed ("just in time"), because loading modules is expensive, especially on Windows. runs.answer: The docs say to use Electron fuses: bits in the binary that you flip at package time, before code signing, so the OS's code-signing checks (Gatekeeper, AppLocker) stop anyone flipping them back. Set them with `@electron/fuses` (`flipFuses`) or `@electron-forge/plugin-fuses`, and check them with `npx @electron/fuses read --app <path>`. Turn off three fuses, all of which are enabled by default: `runAsNode` (`FuseV1Options.RunAsNode`), so `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE` is ignored (this makes `child_process.fork` throw, so use Utility Processes instead); `nodeCliInspect` (`FuseV1Options.EnableNodeCliInspectArguments`), so `--inspect`/`--inspect-brk` are ignored and `SIGUSR1` can't start the main-process inspector; and `nodeOptions` (`FuseV1Options.EnableNodeOptionsEnvironmentVariable`), so `NODE_OPTIONS` and `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` are ignored. Security checklist item 19 explains why: `runAsNode` and `nodeCliInspect` let environment variables or CLI arguments change how the app behaves, which outside scripts can use to run commands on the device with the app's rights. The fuses doc also recommends turning off `grantFileProtocolExtraPrivileges` if you don't serve pages from `file://`, and turning on `embeddedAsarIntegrityValidation` together with `onlyLoadAppFromAsar` so code that hasn't been validated can't be loaded.

runs.answer: Yes: Electron's main-process `safeStorage` module encrypts strings for storage on disk using the operating system's own cryptography. On macOS the key is kept in the Keychain, on Windows it comes from DPAPI, and on Linux it sits in a secret store such as Portal Secret, GNOME libsecret or KWallet. Call `await safeStorage.isAsyncEncryptionAvailable()`, then `await safeStorage.encryptStringAsync(token)` to get a Buffer to write to disk; `await safeStorage.decryptStringAsync(buffer)` returns `{ result, shouldReEncrypt }`, where `shouldReEncrypt` means the key was rotated and the data should be re-encrypted. The synchronous `isEncryptionAvailable`/`encryptString`/`decryptString` methods were removed in Electron 46, but data they encrypted still decrypts with `decryptStringAsync`. Caveats: on Linux with no secret store, the data is encrypted with a hardcoded plaintext password (you can tell when `safeStorage.getSelectedStorageBackend()` returns `basic_text`); on Windows it is not protected from other apps run by the same user; and on macOS the app should be code signed, or the Keychain may ask the user again after every update.

Use Electron's `net` module from the main process, either `net.request(options)` (which returns a `ClientRequest`) or `net.fetch(input[, init])`. Both use Chromium's native networking library rather than Node.js's own `http`/`https` stack or Node's `fetch()`. The docs list automatic management of system proxy configuration as a reason to choose `net` over the Node modules. That includes support for WPAD and PAC files, automatic HTTPS tunneling, and proxies that require basic, digest, NTLM, Kerberos or negotiate authentication. You can only use `net` after the app emits its `ready` event, and `net.fetch` sends requests from the default session (use `ses.fetch()` for a different session).

runs.answer: The BrowserWindow docs ("Showing the window gracefully") give two approaches. First, create the window with `show: false` and call `win.show()` inside `win.once('ready-to-show', ...)`. That event fires once the renderer has rendered the page for the first time, so showing the window then causes no visual flash. It never fires if you set `paintWhenInitiallyHidden: false`. Second, in a complex app where `ready-to-show` could fire too late and make the app feel slow, show the window right away and set `backgroundColor` to something close to your app's background, e.g. `new BrowserWindow({ backgroundColor: '#2e2c29' })`. The docs recommend setting `backgroundColor` even when you also use `ready-to-show`, so the app feels more native. It accepts hex, rgb, hsl or named colors and can also be set with `win.setBackgroundColor()`.

Electron's ABI differs from that of a given Node.js binary (for example, it uses Chromium's BoringSSL instead of OpenSSL), so a native module has to be recompiled for Electron, or loading it throws the 'compiled against a different Node.js version using NODE_MODULE_VERSION' error. The recommended fix is to install modules normally and then rebuild them with @electron/rebuild: run `npm install --save-dev @electron/rebuild`, then run `./node_modules/.bin/electron-rebuild` after every `npm install` (`.\node_modules\.bin\electron-rebuild.cmd` on Windows). It works out the Electron version, downloads the headers and rebuilds the modules, and Electron Forge runs it automatically in development and when making distributables. Other ways: install with npm after setting npm_config_target (the Electron version), npm_config_arch/npm_config_target_arch, npm_config_disturl=https://electronjs.org/headers, npm_config_runtime=electron and npm_config_build_from_source=true (then `HOME=~/.electron-gyp npm install`), or build by hand with `node-gyp rebuild --target=<electron version> --arch=x64 --dist-url=https://electronjs.org/headers`. Troubleshooting says to run @electron/rebuild first when in doubt and to rebuild again after upgrading Electron; the docs don't mention better-sqlite3 by name, so this is their general guidance for any native module.

Since Electron 20, renderers are sandboxed by default unless `nodeIntegration: true` or `sandbox: false` is set. Before that, a renderer with a preload script was unsandboxed by default and its preload had Node.js access. In a sandboxed renderer, the preload's `require` can only load the `electron` module (`contextBridge`, `crashReporter`, `ipcRenderer`, `nativeImage`, `webFrame`, `webUtils`). It cannot load files, Node built-ins or globals like `Buffer`, so requiring an npm package fails. There are two fixes. You can refactor the preload so it doesn't use Node, using Web APIs instead and bundling the npm code (and any polyfills) into one preload file with a bundler such as webpack or Parcel. Or you can set `sandbox: false` for the renderers that need it.

runs.answer: The tray disappears because the variable holding the Tray object gets garbage collected. This usually happens when the Tray is stored in a local variable, for example `const tray = new Tray(...)` inside the `app.whenReady()` callback. Once nothing references it, the garbage collector destroys it and the icon goes away without logging an error. The quick fix is to declare the variable at the top level (`let tray = null`) and assign `tray = new Tray(...)` inside `whenReady()`, so a reference stays alive. The tray tutorial gives the same advice: "save a reference to the Tray object globally to avoid garbage collection." The FAQ also points to articles on memory management and closures.

Electron uses semantic commit messages that follow Conventional Commits. A pull request must have a title with a semantic prefix, and because the repository squash-merges, that title prefix is what counts. The common prefixes are fix: (bug fix), feat: (new feature), docs:, test:, build:, ci:, perf:, refactor: and style: (linting), and the docs also name chore: as a valid type. The first line is a short, lowercase description (preferably 50 characters or fewer, never more than 72), followed by a blank line, with other lines wrapped at 72 columns. A breaking change, which causes a SemVer major bump, is marked by putting `BREAKING CHANGE:` at the start of the commit's optional body or footer, and it can go on a commit of any type (for example fix:, feat: or chore:). The docs describe only this body/footer marker and refer to conventionalcommits.org for more; they do not mention the `!` shorthand used in `chore!:`.

Electron's versioning policy says every supported release line accepts external pull requests that backport fixes already merged to `main`. For some older supported lines, a backport may be accepted only case by case. To backport a fix, you open a backport pull request against each release line that should get it. If a backport to a release line is contested, the Releases Working Group decides it as an agenda item at its weekly meeting in the week the backport PR is raised. This section does not cover any other mechanics, such as tooling or labels.

runs.answer: A fix lands on `main` first. It is then cherry-picked onto the stabilization branch of each supported major version. These branches are named `$MAJOR-x-y` (e.g. `42-x-y`), take only cherry-picked security or stability commits, and are never merged back to `main`. All supported release lines accept pull requests that backport fixes already merged to `main`, though some older supported lines decide case by case. If a backport is contested, the Releases Working Group settles it at its weekly meeting in the week the backport PR is raised. Which lines get a fix follows the support policy: the latest three stable majors are supported, and only the latest minor of each; the newest stable gets every fix from `main`, the one before it gets most fixes as time and bandwidth allow, and the oldest supported line gets only security fixes. The docs don't cover backport tooling, labels, or how to format a batch-backport PR.

runs.answer: According to `ses.registerPreloadScript`, URL filters work like WebExtensions content-script URL matching. A script runs only for a URL that matches at least one `matches` pattern (if set) and at least one `includeGlobs` glob (if set), and matches no `excludeMatches` pattern and no `excludeGlobs` glob; an invalid pattern, or an empty `matches`/`includeGlobs` array, throws an error. `matches`/`excludeMatches` are WebExtensions match patterns, which accept a custom scheme only if it is registered as `standard`. `includeGlobs`/`excludeGlobs` are applied after `matches` and test the whole URL, which is how you filter documents from a non-standard scheme. For `frame` contexts the tested URL is the URL of the document being loaded, with three exceptions: a frame's or popup's initial empty document is matched as `about:blank` (or by its creator's origin when `matchOriginAsFallback` is set), a `data:` URL loaded with `baseURLForDataURL` is matched by its base URL, and a failed navigation's error page is matched by the URL that failed to load (service workers are matched by their scope). The docs list two glob wildcards, `*` (any sequence of characters) and `?`, but they contradict each other on `?`: PreloadScriptRegistration says it matches "zero or one character", while PreloadScript says it matches "any single character".

Do the removal in one merge request. In that MR, add the ~"feature flag" label so release managers know about the removal. If the MR has to be backported into the current version, follow the patch release runbook. Remove every reference to the flag from the codebase, including tests, and delete its YAML definition from the repository. After the MR is merged and deployed to all environments, delete the feature record that is still in the database with `/chatops gitlab run feature delete <feature-flag-name> --dev --pre --staging --staging-ref --production`, then close the flag's rollout issue. Before removing the flag, check that the code is safe during a zero-downtime upgrade. Removing a flag, or setting it to `default_enabled: true`, does not make the code safe on mixed-version nodes, so a flag that guards a data write, cache key or state transition should go through expand-and-contract over three milestones (N expand, N+1 migrate, N+2 remove). Because this is an AI (Duo) flag: if it is pushed to the AI Gateway with `Gitlab::AiGateway.push_feature_flag`, remove it from the AI Gateway repository before GitLab-Rails, or the flag turns off right away in AI Gateway, since disabled is the default there.

runs.answer: A `wip` ("Work In Progress") flag hides a complex feature that is built across several MRs, so the changes can be merged to the main branch before anyone uses the feature. It must not set `default_enabled: true`, can live at most 4 months, does not need an entry on the "All feature flags in GitLab" page, and usually needs no rollout issue, because it should become another type before it is enabled. A `beta` flag is for a feature that GitLab may not yet be able to scale, support and maintain for every use case, or that is not complete enough to be an MVC; the flag lets engineers and customers turn it off. A `beta` flag can set `default_enabled: true`, can live at most 6 months, must appear on the "All feature flags in GitLab" page (generated from the YAML definition) and must have a rollout issue made from the Feature Flag Roll Out template. Change a flag from `wip` once the feature is complete and before it is enabled: choose `beta` or `gitlab_com_derisk` depending on how the feature will be presented and documented to customers, and choose `beta` if it needs to be on by default.

runs.answer: Don't use a regular `db/migrate` migration for this. Regular migrations are for schema changes that run before deploy and should take 3 minutes or less. A data fix that takes "at most a few minutes" (10 minutes or less) goes in a post-deployment migration. runs.answer: The application settings guide says an application_settings column must be removed with the standard column-drop process. That process runs over three releases: ignore the column, drop it, then remove the ignore rule. In release M, add `ignore_column`/`ignore_columns` to the model, with `remove_with` set to M+2 and `remove_after` set to a date after the M+1 release. In the same release, remove every code reference to the column, including model validations, because ActiveRecord caches the table schema when it boots and running processes expect the cached columns to exist. In release M+1, drop the column in a post-deployment migration: a plain transactional `remove_column` works if the column has no indexes or constraints, and otherwise use `disable_ddl_transaction!` with a `down` method that re-adds the column with `if_not_exists: true` and restores its indexes. In release M+2, remove the ignore rule, but only once the `remove_with` release is reached and the `remove_after` date has passed. Never ignore and drop in the same release, because running instances fail when they look up the removed column until the Rails schema cache expires.

Also remove every code reference to the columns, including validations. Release M+1: drop the columns in a post-deployment migration. Update any view that references the column first. Release M+2: remove the ignore rule, but only in the `remove_with` release and after the `remove_after` date. Never ignore and drop in the same release: dropping before ignoring makes running instances fail on the missing column until the schema cache expires, and application_settings.md explicitly requires this ignore → drop → remove-ignore process for application_settings columns.

runs.answer: Change the existing tool in place: don't register a new `register_version`, because MCP clients can't pick a version and `tools/call` always runs the latest one. Keep the change additive. A new optional parameter is fine, but removing a parameter, making one required, or changing what an existing parameter, default or output does is a breaking change under the deprecation guidelines. Custom, aggregated and GraphQL tools are Ruby classes in the `Mcp::Tools` namespace under `app/services/mcp/tools/<domain>/`, registered by `tool_name` in `Mcp::Tools::Manager`. You add the property to the `input_schema` in the class's `register_version`; for GraphQL tools you also pass it on in the `<Operation>Tool#build_variables`, which feeds the `.graphql` file in `app/graphql/queries/mcp/<domain>/`. Tools built from REST endpoints are defined instead by `route_setting :mcp, tool_name:, params: [...]` on the Grape API route, where only the parameters listed in `params:` are accepted and their descriptions come from the route's OpenAPI definition. Rules to follow: keep `project_id`/`url` and internal IDs such as `merge_request_iid` as separate parameters (resolved with the `UrlParser`/`ResourceFinder` concerns), never state a default (`spec/services/mcp/tools/schema_defaults_spec.rb` fails if you do), and either declare the new property in `container_arguments` or list it as never naming a project or group in `ee/spec/lib/ai/tool_rules/governable_tools_container_spec.rb`; the docs mention `save_pipeline` only as a naming example and don't say which file defines it.

runs.answer: MCP server tools are defined in one of two places. REST-backed tools use `route_setting :mcp` on the API route, and its `params:` list filters which inputs are accepted. Class-based tools live under `app/services/mcp/tools/` as `Base::CustomService`, `Base::AggregatedService`, or `Base::GraphqlService` plus `Base::GraphqlTool` (with operations in `app/graphql/queries/mcp/`), registered in `Mcp::Tools::Manager`; the docs name `SavePipelineService` as the save-pipeline service. A class-based tool declares its inputs in the `input_schema` of its `register_version` metadata. To add a parameter, add it as a new optional property in the existing registered version and handle it in the `perform_*` method. Do not register a new version: clients cannot pick a version, `tools/call` always runs the latest, and only additive changes such as a new optional parameter are allowed (making a parameter required or changing what one means is a breaking change). Also follow the conventions: keep `project_id` and the internal ID (such as `merge_request_iid`) as separate parameters, and state no default in the description or schema (`spec/services/mcp/tools/schema_defaults_spec.rb` enforces this). Finally, list the new property in `ee/spec/lib/ai/tool_rules/governable_tools_container_spec.rb`, because every input property must be either a declared container argument or listed as never naming a project or group.

runs.answer: Use `ActiveRecord::QueryRecorder` in a request spec rather than a controller spec, because a controller is only initialized once per example and memoization can make the test pass when it shouldn't. Tag the example `:request_store, :use_sql_query_cache`. Load the page once as a warm-up, then record a control with `control = ActiveRecord::QueryRecorder.new(skip_cached: false) { visit_some_page }`; `skip_cached: false` makes it count cached queries too, so caching can't hide an N+1. Next, add more records (for example `create_list(:issue, 3)`) and assert `expect { visit_some_page }.to issue_same_number_of_queries_as(control)`, which the docs prefer over `exceed_query_limit` because it fails whether the count goes up or down; avoid `.with_threshold(...)` if you can, and if you use it, the extra queries from a regression must exceed the threshold. Create only the records the test needs, but keep them inside the query's filters and page limit so the request actually loads them, and check that the test fails with your fix removed before trusting it.

runs.answer: The docs say to remove a worker class over three minor releases. In release M, remove all code that enqueues the job, such as UI or API paths, and make sure the frontend and backend no longer depend on what the worker did. Also change `perform` so it does nothing but keeps its arguments, so any jobs still in the queue run harmlessly without wasting cycles. In M+1, add a regular migration (not a post-deployment one) that uses `disable_ddl_transaction!` and `sidekiq_remove_jobs(job_klasses: [...])` to clear the remaining jobs from the Sidekiq queues. If the worker is scheduled through sidekiq-cron, the same migration also finds it with `Sidekiq::Cron::Job.find('<schedule.yml key>')` and destroys or disables it, inside `Gitlab::SidekiqSharding::Validator.allow_unrouted_sidekiq_calls`; its `down` method is empty because the removal cannot be undone. In M+2 (this task's step), delete the worker class file and run the Rake tasks from the Sidekiq queues docs to regenerate related files, for example `bin/rake gitlab:sidekiq:all_queues_yml:generate` for `all_queues.yml`.

runs.answer: Removing a worker class is spread over three minor releases. In release M, remove all code that enqueues the job (UI, API and so on), make sure the frontend and backend no longer depend on its work, and turn `perform` into a no-op that keeps the same arguments. Jobs still in the queue then run without doing anything ("avoid unnecessary cycles once any deprecated jobs that are still enqueued eventually get processed"). In M+1, add a regular migration (not a post-deployment one) with `disable_ddl_transaction!` that calls `sidekiq_remove_jobs(job_klasses: [...])` to clear the queues. If the job is scheduled through sidekiq-cron, the same migration also destroys or disables the cron job; its `down` is empty because the removal cannot be undone. In M+2, delete the worker class file and run the Rake tasks from the Sidekiq queues docs (`bin/rake gitlab:sidekiq:all_queues_yml:generate` and `bin/rake gitlab:sidekiq:sidekiq_queues_yml:generate`) to regenerate the queue files.

runs.answer: Don't remove the field. GitLab's GraphQL API is versionless, so you deprecate the field and remove it later through the GitLab deprecation process. There are two steps. First, open a deprecation issue from the `Deprecations` issue template and add the `~GraphQL` and `~deprecation` labels. Second, mark the field in the schema with the `deprecated` property, a Hash of `reason` (why it is deprecated) and `milestone` (the milestone it was deprecated in), for example `deprecated: { reason: 'Use `designCollection`', milestone: '10.0' }`. When a field is being replaced, the `reason` must name the replacement in the form "Use `otherFieldName`" (here, "Use `flowType`"). Keep the original `description` as it is and don't mention the deprecation in it, because the `reason` is added to the end of the description automatically.

runs.answer: Describe every endpoint with the Grape DSL. That means a `desc` summary (starts with a verb, names the resource, a string literal of 120 characters or fewer) with a `detail` string, a `success` (the entity class, `[Entity]` or `is_array: true` for collections, or `code:`/`message:` when there is no body), at least one `failure` array (enforced by the `API/DescriptionFailureResponse` cop), plural `tags` (each described in `tooling/docs/api/tags/<tag>.md`), and a `params` block for validation and coercion. In that block, constrain every String param with `values:`, `limit:` or `regexp:`, and pass params on only through `declared(params, include_parent_namespaces: false).to_h`. Always present the payload with an `API::Entities` class (`present ..., with: Entities::...`). Every exposed field needs a type in its `documentation:` hash (for example `documentation: { type: 'Integer', example: 1 }`), and fields that reference another entity use `using:`. For admin-only access, the endpoint must itself check `authenticated_as_admin!` at request time; if it uses granular-token `route_setting :authorization`, also tag it `assignable_when: [:admin]` (the tag only describes the restriction), and the descriptions should say who can perform the action. The docs say little else specific to admin-only endpoints (no admin-mode spec pattern turned up). For specs, consider a JSON schema fixture in `spec/fixtures/api/schemas` with `expect(response).to match_response_schema(...)`, plus N+1 query tests. Documentation must ship in the same MR (or a follow-up in the same milestone): a Markdown topic under `doc/api` (method and path block, request/response attribute tables, cURL and JSON examples, linked from `api_resources.md` and the global nav), and the OpenAPI definition regenerated with `bin/rake gitlab:openapi:v3:generate`, which the `static-analysis` CI job checks.

runs.answer: Define the endpoint with the Grape DSL: a `desc` summary that starts with a verb and is at most 120 characters, plus `detail`, `success` (the entity, or a `code:`/`model:` hash), at least one `failure` (for example 401/403/404) and plural `tags` with a matching `tooling/docs/api/tags/<tag>.md`. Add a `params` block that limits every String param with `values:`, `limit:` or `regexp:`, pass params on as `declared(params, include_parent_namespaces: false).to_h`, use the status helpers such as `not_found!`, and set a `feature_category`. Always return the payload through an `API::Entities` class (`present ..., with:`) where every `expose` has a `documentation: { type:, example: }` hash and nested entities use `using:`; don't add fields to high-impact entities like `UserBasic`, make a new or feature-bounded entity instead. The docs have no single admin-endpoint checklist, but the granular-token guide says every endpoint needs a `route_setting :authorization` decorator (permission plus a boundary such as `:instance`), and one behind `authenticated_as_admin!` must also be tagged `assignable_when: [:admin]`; the tag only describes the restriction, so the endpoint must still check it (and a `user.admin?` shortcut skips the admin-mode check). Request specs go in `spec/requests/api/` and use `match_response_schema` with a fixture in `spec/fixtures/api/schemas`, a `QueryRecorder` N+1 test for collections, and `it_behaves_like 'authorizing granular token permissions'`; admin calls look like `api(path, admin, admin_mode: true)`. Then run `rake gitlab:permissions:validate` and `gitlab:permissions:routes:compile_docs`. Put the docs in the same merge request: a `doc/api` Markdown topic with history, a `METHOD /api/v4/...` block, request (and response) attribute tables, a cURL example and a JSON response example. Regenerate the OpenAPI definition with `bin/rake gitlab:openapi:v3:generate` and add a changelog entry.

runs.answer: To protect a field, declare an `authorize_granular_token` directive with `permissions:` and a boundary (`boundary_type:` plus `boundary:`, `boundary_argument:` or `boundaries:`). Put it on the type that owns the field, where one directive covers every field on that type, or on the field's resolver, whose directives apply to every field that mounts it. A root query field reads its boundary from an argument with `boundary_argument`. Name the permission after what the type represents or what the action does, not after the schema: object types get `read_<resource>` (for example `IssueType` → `:read_issue`, `ProjectType` → `:read_project`), mutations get `create_`/`update_`/`delete_<resource>`, and special actions get their own permission. The permission must be a raw permission (a YAML file made with `bin/permission`) that belongs to an assignable permission, preferably an existing one, and its `boundary_type` must match that assignable permission's boundaries. Then add the 'authorizing granular token permissions for GraphQL' shared-example spec, run `bundle exec rake gitlab:permissions:graphql:compile_docs` and `bundle exec rake gitlab:permissions:validate`; the docs do not name a specific permission for blame or CODEOWNERS validation.

runs.answer: Declare an `authorize_granular_token` directive with `permissions:` (a symbol or array such as `:read_issue`, named for what is read or done, for example `read_<resource>`). Alongside it, give a boundary: `boundary_type:` (`:project`, `:group`, `:user` or `:instance`) plus either `boundary:` (a method called on the resolved object, or `:itself`), `boundary_argument:` (when the boundary comes from the field's arguments), or `boundaries:` when there are several. The permission must be a raw permission (a YAML file made with `bin/permission`) that belongs to an assignable permission, so that it appears in `Authz::PermissionGroups::Assignable.all_permissions`, and `boundary_type` must match that assignable permission's boundaries; the docs prefer adding it to an existing assignable permission over creating a new one. The directive works on types, mutations and resolvers. For a single field, put it on the field's resolver (a resolver's directives apply to every field that mounts it) or on the field definition with `directives: granular_scope_directive(...)`; a type-level `read_<resource>` already covers all of that type's fields, and when a field returns another authorized type the token needs both types' permissions. Then add the `'authorizing granular token permissions for GraphQL'` shared-example spec and run `bundle exec rake gitlab:permissions:graphql:compile_docs` and `bundle exec rake gitlab:permissions:validate`.

If the store has one module and its actions, getters and mutations total 1000 lines or fewer, use the single-step migration. Otherwise, or if the diff gets too big to review, use the multi-step migration: open a migration issue, add a CODEOWNERS rule, copy the store as-is to a location such as `stores/legacy_store`, create an `index.js` with `defineStore` and the state, then convert the store, migrate its specs, migrate the components, remove Vuex and close the issue. In components, replace `mapActions`/`mapState` with the Pinia versions, `mapMutations` with Pinia's `mapActions` and `mapGetters` with Pinia's `mapState`, and always update the specs in the same change. Component specs should call `Vue.use(PiniaVuePlugin)`, set `pinia = createTestingPinia()` (actions are stubbed by default), create the store (for example `useMyStore()`) before mounting, pass `{ pinia }` to `shallowMount`/`mount`, check that actions were called with the right arguments, and set initial state directly on the store; Pinia actions and their stubs don't return promises, so if a component awaits one, stub it, for example `useMyStore().someAsyncAction.mockResolvedValue()`.

runs.answer: First confirm Pinia is your chosen state manager. Use a single-step migration only if the store has one module and its actions, getters and mutations together stay under 1000 lines; otherwise, or once the diff gets too big to review, use the multi-step migration. The multi-step steps are: copy the Vuex store as-is (for example to `stores/legacy_store`), add a CODEOWNERS rule, create a `defineStore` index holding the state, run the ast-grep codemods (`scripts/frontend/codemods/vuex-to-pinia/migrate.sh path/to/store`), migrate the store specs by hand (using `createTestPiniaAction` and `createCustomGetters` from `helpers/pinia_helpers` only during migration), use `tryStore` only temporarily if stores depend on each other in a circle, refactor the components, and finally remove the Vuex store and the CODEOWNERS rule. In components, replace `mapActions`/`mapState` with the Pinia versions, `mapMutations` with Pinia's `mapActions` and `mapGetters` with Pinia's `mapState`, and always update the specs together with the components. Component specs should call `Vue.use(PiniaVuePlugin)`, create `pinia = createTestingPinia()` (actions are stubbed, and `stubActions: false` is usually not needed), create the store (`useMyStore()`) before mounting, pass `{ pinia }` to `shallowMount`/`mount`, check that actions were called with the right arguments, and set the initial state directly on the store, since stubbed actions cannot set it. Pinia actions don't return promises by default and `createTestingPinia` stubs them, so if a component expects a promise, stub it explicitly, for example `useMyStore().someAsyncAction.mockResolvedValue()`.

runs.answer: Use the `GlSprintf` (`<gl-sprintf>`) component. Keep the whole sentence in one translatable string, and mark the link text with start and end placeholders, for example `s__('ClusterIntegration|Learn more about %{linkStart}zones%{linkEnd}')`. Then render the link in a named slot that receives the wrapped text: `<template #link="{ content }"><gl-link :href="somePath">{{ content }}</gl-link></template>`. The docs say not to split the sentence around a link, either as separate strings or as a bare `%{link}` placeholder whose link text sits outside the translation, because translators then can't adapt word order or grammar. They also say not to put HTML in translation strings. The secure coding guidelines say never to use `v-html` and to use `gl-sprintf` to interpolate translated strings securely.

runs.answer: Per the Prometheus metrics development guidelines, create the metric with `Gitlab::Metrics.histogram`, name it following the Prometheus metric-naming practices, add it to the list of GitLab Prometheus metrics, then trigger the code that records it and check that it appears at `/-/metrics`. Choose labels carefully: high-cardinality values such as `project_path` or `project_id` are strongly discouraged, because each label set becomes a new entry in `/metrics` and buckets multiply that count (a histogram with 10 buckets and a label with 100 values makes 1000 entries). The general guide gives no rule for choosing bucket boundaries. The closest guidance is a Global Search example: the Zoekt tasks histogram `gitlab_search_zoekt_task_duration_seconds` uses buckets `1, 5, 10, 30, 60, 120, 300, 600, 1800, 3600, 7200, 21600` seconds, with an exact `60` edge so that a 60-second objective is read directly from a bucket instead of a quantile interpolated across one. It uses only two bounded labels, `zoekt_node` and `task_type`, but it measures asynchronous indexing tasks, so its range is a pattern to copy rather than a prescription for search request duration.

runs.answer: Following "Adding a new metric", define the metric with `Gitlab::Metrics.histogram` and name it by the Prometheus naming guidelines; the existing Global Search histogram is called `gitlab_search_zoekt_task_duration_seconds`. Add it to the GitLab Prometheus metrics list, then run the code that records it and check that it shows up at `/-/metrics`. Pick labels carefully: high-cardinality values like `project_path` or `project_id` are strongly discouraged, because each label set becomes its own `/metrics` entry and multiplies with the buckets (10 buckets × 100 label values = 1000 entries). Use bounded labels instead, as the Zoekt histogram does with `zoekt_node` and `task_type`. The docs give no general rule for buckets; the only Global Search example is the Zoekt histogram, which is recorded in the same call as its Apdex SLI and uses buckets `1, 5, 10, 30, 60, 120, 300, 600, 1800, 3600, 7200, 21600` seconds, with an exact edge at the 60-second objective so the objective is read straight from a bucket instead of a quantile interpolated across one.

runs.answer: Settings don't cascade by default. In the `NamespaceSetting` model, `include CascadingNamespaceSettingAttribute` and declare the attribute with `cascading_attr :my_setting`. This generates the reader and writer plus `my_setting_locked?`, `_locked_by_ancestor?`, `_locked_by_application_setting?` and `_locked_ancestor`. Then write a migration that includes `Gitlab::Database::MigrationHelpers::CascadingNamespaceSettings` and calls `add_cascading_namespace_setting :my_setting, :boolean, default: false, null: false`, with `remove_cascading_namespace_setting` in `down`. It creates four columns: `my_setting` and `lock_my_setting` in both `namespace_settings` and `application_settings`. Each `lock_` column is a boolean with default false that doesn't allow NULL. The `namespace_settings` value column has no default and allows NULL. Once a group locks the setting, the reader returns that ancestor's value, or a locked instance value, before the group's own value. Otherwise it falls back to the nearest non-nil ancestor, then the instance setting. `_locked?` returns false on the group that did the locking unless you pass `include_self: true`, which you would do when checking from a project. For projects, the doc says to add the cascading setting to the `project_settings` table instead of reusing `namespace_settings`. Its example link reads "MR 149931" but points to !144931. For a Duo/AI setting that cascades on write, also: add it to `update_cascading_settings` in `ee/app/services/ee/groups/update_service.rb`; add it to the allowed list in `ee/app/services/ai/cascade_duo_settings_service.rb`; and add it to `DUO_CASCADING_SETTINGS` in `EE::Projects::CreateService`, so new projects get the group's value even when the column is `NOT NULL DEFAULT`.

runs.answer: Declare the attribute in the `NamespaceSetting` model with `cascading_attr :your_setting` (the model includes `CascadingNamespaceSettingAttribute`). This generates the reader and writer plus `_locked?`, `_locked_by_ancestor?`, `_locked_by_application_setting?` and `_locked_ancestor`, and the reader returns a locked ancestor's or instance value before the group's own value, then the nearest ancestor that isn't nil, then the application setting. For a brand-new setting, write a migration that includes `Gitlab::Database::MigrationHelpers::CascadingNamespaceSettings` and calls `add_cascading_namespace_setting :name, :type, default: ..., null: false` (with `remove_cascading_namespace_setting` in `down`). That creates a value column and a `lock_<name>` boolean column in both `namespace_settings` and `application_settings`. If you convert an existing setting, add these columns by hand: in `namespace_settings`, a nullable value column with no default and a `lock_` boolean (default false, not null); in `application_settings`, a value column of the same type with a default, not null, plus its `lock_` boolean. Project-level cascading settings go in `project_settings` rather than `namespace_settings` (the example is MR 144931; its link text says 149931). For new settings the docs recommend real defaults and cascade-on-write through async workers: for AI/Duo settings, add the setting to `update_cascading_settings` in `ee/app/services/ee/groups/update_service.rb`, to the allowed list in `ee/app/services/ai/cascade_duo_settings_service.rb`, and to `DUO_CASCADING_SETTINGS` in `EE::Projects::CreateService` so new projects inherit the group value; the UI lock/enforcement checkbox comes from `cascading_namespace_setting_locked?`, the HAML partials, or `cascading_lock_icon.vue`.

runs.answer: Yes, if `deployments` is an organization table, because then a real foreign key to `users` would cross databases. The docs don't give `deployments`' schema; the multiple databases doc says a table's schema is marked in its `db/docs/<table>.yml` file. By default the docs want a real foreign key whenever a table references another table or a model gets an association: add an index first, and set ON DELETE CASCADE in 99% of cases. A loose foreign key is for references PostgreSQL cannot enforce because parent and child are in different databases or schemas. It is an entry in `config/gitlab_loose_foreign_keys.yml` (`async_delete` or `async_nullify`) plus a DELETE-tracking trigger on the parent, and a worker cleans up orphaned rows later rather than immediately. `users` is in the `gitlab_main_user` schema, and the docs' own example says a `gitlab_main_org` table's `user_id` → `users` "is now treated as a cross-database foreign key" (`notification_settings`, later converted to a loose foreign key); `no_cross_db_foreign_keys_spec.rb` fails on a new one, and the allowlist is only for foreign keys that already exist. With a loose foreign key, the application must check the parent exists when creating a record (look up the user rather than trusting a raw ID); the column then passes `spec/db/schema_spec.rb` without being added to `ignored_fk_columns_map`, and the docs strongly advise the `scripts/decomposition/generate-loose-foreign-key` script for swapping an existing foreign key.

runs.answer: The docs make a real foreign key the default: any column that references another table gets an FK, with its index added first and usually ON DELETE CASCADE, so PostgreSQL enforces consistency. Loose foreign keys are for when that can't work, because the two tables sit in different databases or in `gitlab_schema`s that may not have FKs between them; cleanup then happens later, through a DELETE trigger on the parent and a worker that applies `async_delete`/`async_nullify` as set in `config/gitlab_loose_foreign_keys.yml`. `users` is in the `gitlab_main_user` schema, and the docs' own example (`notification_settings.user_id` → `users`, once that table moved to the organization schema) counts such a reference as a cross-database FK that `no_cross_db_foreign_keys_spec.rb` rejects and that should become a loose FK. So if `deployments` is an organization (`gitlab_main_org`) table, as project data normally is, `deployments.user_id` should be a loose FK (the docs even show `table: users, column: user_id, on_delete: async_nullify`), and a hard FK is right only when both schemas allow FKs between them (for example, cell-local tables may hard-reference `gitlab_main_org`/`gitlab_main_user`). With a loose FK the application must check the parent exists before creating rows, look up records through the parent, and handle parents that are already deleted; the docs never mention `deployments.user_id` or say which schema `deployments` is in, so check `db/docs/deployments.yml`.

runs.answer: The Sharding guidelines say every row of an organization-level table (gitlab_schema gitlab_main_org, gitlab_main_user, gitlab_ci, gitlab_sec or gitlab_shared_org) needs exactly one sharding key. That key must be as specific as possible, non-nullable and immutable. Use `project_id` (pointing to `projects`) when rows belong to a project, and `namespace_id`/`group_id` (pointing to `namespaces`) when they belong to a group or namespace, but not when the namespace could be a user namespace, because that can be NULL. Use `organization_id` only for root-level models that do not belong to a project or namespace. It is not for leaf-level models, tables holding group or project data, or very large tables, because moving an organization rewrites every row. It also needs Tenant Scale group approval, transfer-service support and common-organization factory defaults. If the value can come from a parent table the table already references, fill it from that parent with `desired_sharding_key.backfill_via.parent` instead of adding a second foreign key. The key is declared as `sharding_key` (for example `sharding_key: {project_id: projects}`) in the table's `db/docs/` file, and the docs give no ruling specific to deploy_keys, so you apply these general rules.

Cell-local tables must not have one. Each row needs exactly one sharding key, and it should be the most specific owner that is non-null and never changes: `project_id` (→ projects) if the rows belong to a project, otherwise `namespace_id`/`group_id` (→ namespaces) if they belong to a group, but not where the namespace could be a personal UserNamespace, because the value can be NULL. `organization_id` is a fallback only for tables that belong to neither a project nor a namespace. You declare the key in the table's database dictionary file under `db/docs/` (for example `sharding_key:\n  project_id: projects`), and only once the column has a NOT NULL constraint. Until then use `desired_sharding_key`, with `backfill_via.parent` when the value comes from a parent table, and fill the column in the model with `populate_sharding_key`. runs.answer: Every Sidekiq worker must explicitly set `data_consistency` (a RuboCop rule enforces this), and `:sticky` is the preferred option: the job prefers replicas but switches to the primary for writes or when it hits replication lag, so use it for jobs that need to run as fast as possible. Jobs are enqueued with the current database LSN, so for `:sticky` (and `:delayed`) the replica is guaranteed to be caught up to the point the job was enqueued; otherwise the job is retried or uses the primary. Use `:delayed` only when further delay doesn't matter, such as cache expiration or web hook execution. If the replica is lagging before the job starts, a `:delayed` job is retried once and then falls back to the primary, so never use it for jobs with retries disabled, such as cron jobs. `:always` sends every query to the primary; it is strongly discouraged and only needed for jobs that hit edge cases around primary stickiness.

runs.answer: Use `:sticky` for jobs that need to run as fast as possible. The docs call it the preferred option. A sticky job reads from replicas but switches to the primary for writes, or as soon as it hits replication lag. Jobs are enqueued with the current database LSN, so replicas are guaranteed to have caught up to the point at which the job was enqueued. Use `:delayed` instead only when extra delay does not matter, such as cache expiration or web hooks execution. On replication lag it retries the job once and then falls back to the primary, so it must not be used for jobs with retry disabled, such as cron jobs. `:always` (primary for every query) is strongly discouraged and is only needed for jobs that hit edge cases around primary stickiness.

runs.answer: If an outgoing request includes user-supplied information, you must check where it is going. The docs prefer three SSRF fixes, in this order: connect only to known, trusted domains or IP addresses; send the request through the `Gitlab::HTTP` wrapper; or, only if neither is possible, build fixes into the feature itself and have AppSec review them. `Gitlab::HTTP` hands requests to the `gitlab-http` gem, guards against every SSRF route GitLab knows about, and follows the instance's "Outbound requests" settings that can block internal connections. To check a URL, use `Gitlab::HTTP_V2::UrlBlocker` (or `AddressableUrlValidator` / `public_url`). With `dns_rebind_protection: true` you must use the URI it returns, with the hostname replaced by an IP; a URL that passed validation when the record was saved must be checked again before it is used. For KubeClient specifically, the Kubernetes guide adds: pass `http_max_redirects: 0` to block redirects, and never show raw error messages (use `e.error_code`).

runs.answer: The secure coding guidelines say you must validate the destination of any outgoing request that includes user-supplied data. They list the preferred SSRF mitigations in order: connect only to known, trusted domains or IPs; otherwise use the `Gitlab::HTTP` library; otherwise build feature-specific mitigations that AppSec reviews (block localhost, private RFC 1918 and link-local addresses, disable or validate redirects, and validate then use the first resolved IP). `Gitlab::HTTP` hands requests to the `gitlab-http` gem, covers every SSRF vector GitLab knows about, and follows the admin "Outbound requests" settings that block internal connections. For third-party gems, configuring `Gitlab::HTTP` as their HTTP connection library is preferred over writing the mitigations again. If you validate with `Gitlab::HTTP_V2::UrlBlocker` and `dns_rebind_protection: true`, you must use the safe URI it returns, with the hostname replaced by the resolved IP; ignoring that return value leaves DNS rebinding (TOCTOU) open, and for KubeClient, whose cluster URLs are user-controlled, the Kubernetes doc also says to pass `http_max_redirects: 0` and never expose raw error messages.

runs.answer: Use structured JSON logging, not `Rails.logger` or `$stdout`. In the service, include `::Gitlab::Loggable` and log through a memoized `Gitlab::AppJsonLogger.build`, wrapping the payload in `build_structured_payload(...)` so a `class` attribute is added automatically. Only create a new `Gitlab::JsonLogger` subclass (a new log file) if no existing log fits, and check with a maintainer first. Put context into separate fields next to a `message:` key, without interpolating values into the message string, for example `logger.info(build_structured_payload(message: 'log message', project_id: project_id))`, and keep a common set of base fields such as `current_user_id` and `project_id`. Keep each field's type the same everywhere (for example, separate `error_code: 1` and `error: "I/O failure"` keys, never one key with mixed types; list elements of one type), and log durations as float seconds in keys that contain `duration` and end in `_s` (for example `view_duration_s`). The docs say nothing specific about "log-only" checks, so this general guidance is what applies, along with the rule that new logs must not grow overall log volume by more than 10%.

runs.answer: Each workload (a Rails request or Sidekiq job) gets a fresh `Session` for each load-balanced database. `ConnectionProxy` then routes each connection request using these checks in order: writes go to the primary and mark the session as written; a session already stuck to the primary stays there; `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` and other locking reads go to the primary, and so do queries inside an active `use_primary` block; everything else goes to a replica, but only one that `LoadBalancer` has found close enough to the primary. Transactions also go to the primary by default. After a write, the request sticks to the primary. Redis tracks this by PostgreSQL LSN, and for web requests the stick is keyed on `(:user, current user ID)`; it is released when a replica catches up to the write LSN or after 30 seconds. To force a primary read, wrap the queries in a `use_primary` block, which sends every query in it to the primary, or call `use_primary!` to stick the session to the primary for the rest of the request. The docs name these blocks (namespace `Gitlab::Database::LoadBalancing`) but don't show the exact code to call them.

runs.answer: Each workload, such as a Rails web request, gets a fresh `Session` for each load-balanced database. When ActiveRecord asks for a connection, `ConnectionProxy` checks these rules in order: a write (insert, update or delete) goes to the primary and marks the session as written; a session already stuck to the primary stays there; a locking read such as `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` goes to the primary; any query inside an active `use_primary` block goes to the primary; everything else goes to a replica. Transactions use the primary by default. After a write, the request sticks to the primary. For web requests this is scoped to (namespace `:user`, current user ID) and tracked in Redis using LSN positions. The stick ends when a replica catches up to the write's LSN or after 30 seconds. Replicas that lag too much are skipped, and reads fall back to the primary if every replica is offline. To force a primary read, wrap the queries in a `use_primary` block, which sends every query in the block to the primary, or call `use_primary!`, which sticks the session to the primary for the rest of the workload.

runs.answer: Automatic deferral works like the throttling in batched background migrations. A worker opts in by calling `defer_on_database_health_signal` with a `gitlab_schema`, `tables` (used only by the autovacuum indicator) and `delay_by` (5 seconds by default). If the schema and tables aren't known in advance, you can pass a block instead: it receives the job arguments, schema and tables and returns `[schema, tables]`, and the middleware runs it when it fetches the job from the queue. The first deferral delays the job by `delay_by`. While the stop signal persists, each later deferral doubles the delay, minus up to 10% random jitter, up to a 30-minute maximum. This doubling sits behind the `incremental_database_health_defer_delay` feature flag, which is off by default. Logs show `job_status: deferred`, `job_deferred_by: database_health_check` and `deferred_count`. By default the middleware checks `Gitlab::Database::HealthStatus::DEFAULT_INDICATORS`, which are `AutovacuumActiveOnTable`, `WriteAheadLog`, `PatroniApdex` and `WalRate`. You can pass `indicators:` to check fewer, for example `GLOBAL_INDICATORS` (only `WriteAheadLog`, `PatroniApdex` and `WalRate`), so that autovacuum on the worker's tables does not defer it, as `Projects::TransferWorker` does. A worker can also override `self.defer_on_database_health_signal?` to control when deferral applies, for example to put it behind a feature flag.

Every field adds 1 to a query's complexity score by default, and the total is checked against limits defined as constants in app/graphql/gitlab_schema.rb. Queries are also limited by depth and recursion. A field can override the default with a custom graphql-ruby `complexity` value: give a higher value to a field that makes the server do more work, and 0 to a near-free field such as `id` or `title`. Complexity can also be set per object, and the final query complexity is based on how many objects are returned, so expensive objects (for example ones that need Gitaly calls) cost more. A resolver can adjust its own cost by overriding `self.resolver_complexity(args, child_complexity:)`: it calls `super` and adds to the result, for example `complexity += 2 if args[:label_name]`. The full rules are on the client-facing API page and in the graphql-ruby complexity docs, which are not in this index.

runs.answer: GitLab's GraphQL API gives each query a complexity score so it can reject overly complex queries. The limits are constants in `app/graphql/gitlab_schema.rb`. By default every field adds `1` to the score. A field can set a custom `complexity` (a graphql-ruby feature) instead: use a higher value for fields that make the server do more work, and `0` for cheap fields such as `id` or `title`. Marking a field `calls_gitaly: true` adds `1` to that field's complexity. Complexity can also be set per object, and the final score depends on how many objects the query returns. A resolver can change its contribution with `def self.resolver_complexity(args, child_complexity:)`, which calls `super` and adds to the result, for example `complexity += 2 if args[:label_name]`. Raising a field's complexity or a resolver's multipliers counts as a breaking change, but lowering them does not. The detailed explanation of how the score is computed is on the client-facing page `../api/graphql/_index.md#maximum-query-complexity`, which sits outside the allowed `doc/development` folder, so I did not read it.

Order matters, but at the rule level the framework sets it, not the order you write rules in. When `policy.allowed?(:ability)` is called, DeclarativePolicy picks only the rules relevant to that ability, uses short-circuiting so it does not have to compute every condition, and sorts the rules by how expensive they are to compute. That sorting is dynamic and cache-aware: conditions already computed are considered first. The developer gives a condition its cost through the `score:` parameter on `condition`, and `policy.debug(:ability)` prints the rules in the order they are evaluated, with their scores. Inside a single condition block, the Ruby is evaluated as written, so the review guidelines say to put cheap checks first, run queries last and guard against a nil user (for example `@user.present? && @subject.widgets_enabled? && @subject.members.exists?(...)`).

runs.answer: The `* as-if-foss` jobs run in the same merge request pipeline as the regular EE-context jobs. They run the GitLab test suite as if it were running in `gitlab-org/gitlab-foss`. To do that, they set the `FOSS_ONLY='1'` CI/CD variable and remove the EE-only paths before the tests start. Those paths are listed in `.gitlab/ee-only-paths.txt`, and the shared `.as-if-foss` CI template is what sets `FOSS_ONLY='1'`. A separate cross-project downstream FOSS pipeline runs inside the FOSS project and removes the same paths by simulating a merge into its default branch. `merge-train` reads that same list when it syncs gitlab-org/gitlab to gitlab-foss. The jobs run when the MR has the `pipeline:run-as-if-foss` label (or `pipeline:as-if-foss-run-predictive`), when the MR is in the security project, or when CI config files change.

runs.answer: `Rails.cache` uses the cache Redis instance (`redis-cluster-cache` on GitLab.com). `Gitlab::Redis::Cache` uses that same instance, and in the GDK and most other environments all Redis uses point to one instance. That instance can have an LRU key-eviction policy, so entries can be deleted before they expire: use it only for data that can be regenerated, and use `Gitlab::Redis::SharedState` for data that must persist. Key conventions: build names from colon-separated parts such as `projects:1:somekey`, keep them unique across all Redis categories (the default Omnibus and GDK setups share one server), and use IDs that never change (project ID, not full path). When an operation needs several keys on the same Redis Cluster node, wrap the varying part in curly braces, as in `project:{1}:set_a`. Expiry: `Rails.cache` has a default TTL of 8 hours, and the docs suggest 8 hours for general caching because it matches a workday; `Gitlab::Redis::Cache` has no default TTL, so you must always set one. Rails prefers TTLs and changing cache keys (for example `cache_key_with_version`, which includes `updated_at`) over explicit deletes, and the docs say to contact `#g_durability` before adding a large cache workload.
