runs.answer: `Rails.cache` uses Redis as its store. In most environments, including the GDK and default Omnibus, every Redis use shares one instance, but on GitLab.com the cache has its own instance, `redis-cluster-cache` (a Redis Cluster). That instance is set up with LRU key eviction and is the same one `Gitlab::Redis::Cache` uses, so entries can disappear before their TTL: use it only for truly cache-like data that can be regenerated, and use `Gitlab::Redis::SharedState` (no eviction) for data that must persist. Key conventions: separate parts with colons (for example `projects:1:somekey`), keep keys unique across all Redis uses, and build them from IDs that never change (project ID, not full path). Where a multi-key command needs several keys on the same cluster node, put the shared part in curly braces (for example `project:{1}:set_a`). Expiry: set the TTL with `expires_in`. `Rails.cache` defaults to 8 hours, which the docs recommend for general caching because it matches a workday; use a shorter expiry for large data, a low `race_condition_ttl` (about 10 seconds) for heavily used keys, and always set a TTL explicitly when writing through `Gitlab::Redis::Cache`, which has no default.

An import starts with `POST /import/github`. The call chain is `Import::GitHubService` → `Gitlab::LegacyGithubImport::ProjectCreator` → `Projects::CreateService` → `@project.import_state.schedule` → `project.add_import_job`, which enqueues `RepositoryImportWorker`. That worker runs `Projects::ImportService`, whose importer for `github` is `ParallelImporter`, and `ParallelImporter` schedules the first stage. The stages then run in this order: `Stage::ImportRepositoryWorker` (repository and wiki); `Stage::ImportBaseDataWorker` (labels, milestones and releases, single-threaded); `Stage::ImportPullRequestsWorker` (one `ImportPullRequestWorker` job per pull request); `Stage::ImportCollaboratorsWorker` (optional but on by default, one `ImportCollaboratorWorker` job per collaborator); `Stage::ImportIssuesAndDiffNotesWorker` (`ImportIssueWorker` per issue, `DiffNoteImporter` jobs for pull request comments); `Stage::ImportIssueEventsWorker` (`ImportIssueEventWorker` per event, with review-request events replayed in order by `ReplayEventsWorker`); `Stage::ImportAttachmentsWorker` (optional, Releases/Notes/Issues/MergeRequests attachment importers); `Stage::ImportProtectedBranchesWorker` (`ImportProtectedBranchWorker` per rule); and `Stage::FinishImportWorker` (housekeeping, then marks the import complete). A stage that does all its work in one thread schedules the next stage directly. Every other stage schedules `Gitlab::GithubImport::AdvanceStageWorker`, which checks the `Gitlab::JobWaiter` Redis keys and reschedules itself until the stage's jobs finish, then refreshes the import JID and schedules the next stage. These workers use the `github_importer` and `github_importer_advance_stage` queues, and the JID is refreshed during the import (`ProjectImportState#refresh_jid_expiration` or `RefreshImportJidWorker`) so `StuckProjectImportJobsWorker` does not mark long imports as failed.

runs.answer: The GitHub importer is a parallel importer built on Sidekiq, and its jobs run on the `github_importer` and `github_importer_advance_stage` queues. A `POST /import/github` request goes through `Import::GitHubService`, `Gitlab::LegacyGithubImport::ProjectCreator`, `Projects::CreateService`, `import_state.schedule` and `project.add_import_job`, which enqueues `RepositoryImportWorker`. That worker runs `Projects::ImportService`, whose importer for the `github` type is `ParallelImporter`, and it schedules the stage workers in this order: `Stage::ImportRepositoryWorker` (repository and wiki), `Stage::ImportBaseDataWorker` (labels, milestones and releases, in one thread), `Stage::ImportPullRequestsWorker` (one `ImportPullRequestWorker` job per pull request), `Stage::ImportCollaboratorsWorker` (optional, one `ImportCollaboratorWorker` job per collaborator), `Stage::ImportIssuesAndDiffNotesWorker` (`ImportIssueWorker` per issue, `DiffNoteImporter` jobs for pull request comments), `Stage::ImportIssueEventsWorker` (`ImportIssueEventWorker` per event, with review-request events replayed in order by `ReplayEventsWorker`), `Stage::ImportAttachmentsWorker` (optional, attachment importers for releases, notes, issues and merge requests), `Stage::ImportProtectedBranchesWorker` (`ImportProtectedBranchWorker` per rule), and finally `Stage::FinishImportWorker` (housekeeping such as flushing caches, then marks the import complete). A stage moves to the next one in one of two ways: a single-threaded stage schedules the next worker directly, and any other stage schedules `Gitlab::GithubImport::AdvanceStageWorker`. That worker gets the project ID, the `Gitlab::JobWaiter` Redis keys and the next stage's name, and it reschedules itself until the stage's jobs are done. It then refreshes the import job ID and schedules the next stage.

runs.answer: By default, GitLab does not deduplicate jobs scheduled with a delay. It assumes the state will have changed by the time the job runs, so a delayed duplicate is not dropped even if a matching job is still pending. You have to turn on deduplication of scheduled jobs per worker by passing `including_scheduled: true` when declaring the strategy, for example `deduplicate :until_executing, including_scheduled: true` together with `idempotent!`. This works with both the `until_executing` and `until_executed` strategies. In general, a job for an idempotent worker is deduplicated when an unstarted job with the same arguments is already in the queue.

runs.answer: No, not by default. GitLab doesn't skip jobs that are scheduled to run in the future, because it assumes the state will have changed by the time they run, so a delayed duplicate is still enqueued. You can turn deduplication on for scheduled jobs by passing `including_scheduled: true` to the deduplication strategy, for example `deduplicate :until_executing, including_scheduled: true`. This works with both the `until_executing` strategy (the default, which releases the lock before the job starts) and the `until_executed` strategy (which releases it after the job finishes). Normal deduplication only applies to idempotent workers (`idempotent!`): a second job is dropped while an unstarted job with the same arguments is already in the queue, and the Redis idempotency key has a TTL of 10 minutes by default, which you can change with `ttl:`.

When files in `/doc` change in a merge request, Danger Bot posts documentation guidelines, and that rule is configured in `danger/documentation/Dangerfile`. Each Danger task has its own `danger/<task-name>/Dangerfile`. Shared or complex logic goes in plugins under `danger/plugins/...`, which include modules from `tooling/danger/...`. To test locally, run `bin/rake danger_local`, which runs a subset of the current checks; a `Dangerfile` itself can't be tested directly, so put the logic in `tooling/danger/...` and cover it with RSpec specs in `spec/tooling/danger/...`. To confirm the `Dangerfile` itself works, you must push the branch to GitLab; emptying `.gitlab/ci/rails.gitlab-ci.yml` in your MR makes those CI runs faster, but revert that before merging.

The docs don't describe a separate `Gemfile.checksum` file to edit. GitLab moved to Bundler's built-in checksum verification in GitLab 19.0, and the old `bundler-checksum` gem was removed in GitLab 19.3. Now `bundle install` updates the `CHECKSUMS` section in `Gemfile.lock` automatically, so run it after the version bump and include the updated `Gemfile.lock` in your change. Because `Gemfile.lock` changed, also run `bundle exec rake bundler:gemfile:sync` to keep `Gemfile.next.lock` in step, then review and commit the changes to `Gemfile.next.lock`. The docs don't mention the CI error message itself.

runs.answer: `fast_spec_helper` skips gem loading, the Rails app boot, GitLab Shell and Gitaly setup, and test repository setup. It does autoload classes from `lib/` and loads all ActiveSupport extensions, including core extensions, so code that uses only `lib/` needs no explicit requires. If the code uses gems or depends on something outside `lib/`, load it with `require_dependency`. The preferred place is the library file that needs it, for example `require_dependency 're2'` for code calling `Gitlab::UntrustedRegexp`; adding it to the spec itself also works. If many `fast_spec_helper` specs in a domain need the same dependency, create `spec/support/fast_spec/YOUR_DOMAIN/fast_spec_helper_support.rb` and require it from `fast_spec_helper`. To check isolation, run the spec on its own with `bin/rspec`, not `bin/spring rspec`, which loads `spec_helper` automatically; `scripts/run-fast-specs.sh` helps find `fast_spec_helper` specs that fail when run alone.

Don't read the element's state once and compare it, for example with `find(...).value`, `.text`, `all(...).count` or `page.current_url`. That captures the page at one moment and races any async update still rendering. Instead, assert with Capybara's waiting `have_*` matchers, which retry until the expectation holds: for example `expect(page).to have_field('id', with: value)`, `have_selector(selector, count:/exact_text:)`, `have_css`, `have_content` or `have_current_path`. Only when there is no UI outcome to assert on, use the `wait_for('description', max_wait_time:, polling_interval:) { condition }` helper from `spec/support/helpers/wait_helpers.rb` as a last resort; to retry an interaction that isn't ready yet, wrap it in `wait_for` and rescue `Capybara::ElementNotFound`. Never use `wait_for_requests` or `wait_for_all_requests` in feature specs: the `RSpec/AvoidWaitForRequests` cop forbids them, and you must not add todo exclusions or disable the cop inline. Note that the feature-spec guidance names values, text, counts and URLs, not attributes or `sleep` by name, so applying it to an attribute like `href` is an extension of the rule.

runs.answer: In feature (`:js`) specs, use Capybara's waiting `have_*` matchers instead of reading an element's value directly. Reading a value, text or count with `find(...)` or `all(...)` captures the page at one moment and can catch it mid-update. The `have_*` matchers retry until the expectation holds or the wait times out. For a link's href, the docs' Matchers example is `expect(page).to have_link _('UI testing docs'), href: docs_url # assert the link has an href`, and `have_selector(..., count:)` and `have_field(..., with:)` work the same way. Use the `wait_for` helper (`spec/support/helpers/wait_helpers.rb`, with optional `max_wait_time` and `polling_interval`) only as a last resort, when nothing visible in the UI can be asserted on; `evaluate_script` and `execute_script` don't wait either. Never use `wait_for_requests` or `wait_for_all_requests`, because the `RSpec/AvoidWaitForRequests` cop prohibits them; the feature-spec docs don't mention `sleep` itself, but the end-to-end Waits page calls a fixed `sleep` an unreliable readiness signal.

runs.answer: The limit is 30: `GitalyClient` raises `Gitlab::GitalyClient::TooManyInvocationsError` when Gitaly is called more than 30 times in a single Rails request or Sidekiq execution. This check runs during development and testing to catch n+1 calls. For a quick local workaround you can export `GITALY_DISABLE_REQUEST_LIMITS=1`, which turns off n+1 detection in your environment. The real fix is to find the n+1, which is usually a loop that calls Gitaly once for each element of an array, and to raise an issue labelled ~Gitaly ~performance ~"technical debt" with the full stack trace, the error message and the failing tests (ask the Gitaly Team if you can't find the source). Once you have found it, wrap that code in `Gitlab::GitalyClient.allow_n_plus_1_calls do ... end` with a `# n+1: <issue link>` comment, which removes that code path from n+1 detection. The docs don't mention ListRefs by name, so this is general guidance.

`GitalyClient` raises `Gitlab::GitalyClient::TooManyInvocationsError` to catch n+1 problems. It fires when Gitaly is called more than 30 times in a single Rails request or Sidekiq execution, and that limit is the constant `Gitlab::GitalyClient::MAXIMUM_GITALY_CALLS`. As a temporary measure you can `export GITALY_DISABLE_REQUEST_LIMITS=1`, which turns off n+1 detection in your development environment. The documented fix has three steps. First, raise an issue labelled ~Gitaly ~performance ~"technical debt" that includes the full stack trace, the error message and any failing tests. Second, find the source of the n+1, which is usually a loop that calls Gitaly once for each element of an array. Third, wrap that code in `Gitlab::GitalyClient.allow_n_plus_1_calls do ... end` with a `# n+1: <issue link>` comment, which excludes that code path from n+1 detection. Separately, the docs say Gitaly fetches can be batched like database queries. You can guard against a regression with a `:request_store` spec that checks `Gitlab::GitalyClient.get_request_count` changes `by(n)`. The docs say nothing specific about ListRefs.

runs.answer: Scaffold new tests with the repo's generator, `pnpm new-test`. The docs say using it is mandatory, and it sets up the right structure with fixture files. It is interactive by default, so agents should run it non-interactively as `pnpm new-test --args <appDir> <name> <type>`. `--args` is a `turbo gen` flag, so pass it directly with no `--` separator. `appDir` is true or false (whether the test is for the app directory), `name` is the test name (e.g. `my-feature`), and `type` is one of `e2e`, `production`, `development` or `unit`, as in `pnpm new-test --args true my-feature e2e`. A unit test is created as a flat `test/unit/<name>.test.ts` and ignores `appDir` (e.g. `pnpm new-test --args false my-util unit`), but the docs say to prefer integration tests (e2e, development, production) over unit tests.

runs.answer: Use `retry()` from `next-test-utils` instead of `setTimeout` (or fixed sleeps like `await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 1000))`). Put the assertion inside the callback so it polls until it passes, for example `await retry(async () => { const text = await browser.elementByCss('p').text(); expect(text).toBe('expected value') })`. Don't use the older `check()` helper, which is deprecated; use `retry()` with `expect()` instead.

runs.answer: If your changes are only in core Next.js files (`packages/next/**`), rebuild with `pnpm --filter=next build` (about 60s) before running integration tests. Use `pnpm build` if JS changed across multiple packages, and `pnpm build-all` only if Turbopack or other Rust code changed. Yes, there is a watch mode: `pnpm --filter=next dev` rebuilds automatically when files change (about 1-2s per change). The default agent rule is to start it in a separate terminal before editing Next.js source (or say explicitly why you skipped it), run focused tests with the script for your mode, such as `pnpm test-dev-turbo test/path/to/test.ts`, and stop the watcher when you're done. If you only need to check for type errors, `pnpm --filter=next types` (about 10s) is faster than a full build.

The docs already say that setting up a new clone or worktree does not require `pnpm build-all`. Run `pnpm install`, which already pulls in recent published native bindings, so no Rust build is needed. After that, build only what your work changes: `pnpm --filter=next build` if you only edit core Next.js files, `pnpm build` if your changes span several JS packages, and `pnpm build-all` only if they include Rust/Turbopack code. Changes to tests alone need no framework rebuild before pushing to CI. The fast watch-mode workflow (`pnpm --filter=next dev`) assumes the workspace is already set up and its framework build outputs are current, so missing or outdated outputs still need a build; switching branches or pulling may also need `pnpm build` for JS or `pnpm build-all` for Rust, and if Next.js then fails to start, the published native bindings may be behind canary (see the docs' Stale Native Binary section).

Run `pnpm install`, which already pulls in recent published native (SWC/Turbopack) bindings, then build only what your work changes: `pnpm --filter=next build` if edits are limited to core Next.js files (`packages/next/**`), `pnpm build` if changes span multiple JS packages, and `pnpm build-all` only if changes include Rust/Turbopack code. runs.answer: Before you commit, run on your changed files exactly what the pre-commit hook (lint-staged) runs. That catches problems early and avoids slow lint-staged failures, which take about 2 minutes each. First format with `pnpm prettier --with-node-modules --ignore-path .prettierignore --write <files>`. Then lint and auto-fix with `npx eslint --config eslint.config.mjs --fix <files>`. In both commands, replace `<files>` with the paths you changed.

The recommended way is `git node v8 backport <hash>` (install `@node-core/utils` and the git-node-v8 prerequisites, and run it on a branch made from the branch you are targeting). It updates a local V8 clone, generates the patch, then applies and commits it to deps/v8 and increments the embedder version number; if there are conflicts, you resolve and stage them, then type RESOLVED. To do it by hand, run `curl -L https://github.com/v8/v8/commit/<hash>.patch | git am -3 --directory=deps/v8`, then `git commit --amend --reset-author` to rewrite the message in the V8 backport format: `deps: cherry-pick <hash> from V8 upstream`, an indented "Original commit message:", `Refs:` linking the upstream V8 commit, and `PR-URL:`. Besides the patched deps/v8 files, you must increase the `v8_embedder_string` number in `common.gypi` (git-node does this for you); then open the PR, notify `@nodejs/v8`, and run the V8 CI as well as the normal Node.js CI. For `main` specifically, the docs say not to cherry-pick single V8 patches unless the patch fixes a build issue on a supported platform or toolchain, fixes a security issue, or unblocks a pending V8 update; otherwise wait for the next V8 update.

Node's bundled zlib does not come from standard zlib. It comes from the Chromium team's zlib fork (chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/refs/heads/main/third_party/zlib), which has performance improvements that standard zlib lacks. Like most dependencies, it is updated automatically by the dependency-update-action, which runs weekly. To update it by hand, run the matching script in `tools/update-deps`, although other guides in the same docs (merve, OpenSSL) give the script directory as `tools/dep_updaters`. A manual-update PR is accepted only if the automated tooling cannot produce the update, the reason is clearly documented, and the PR is either reviewed in detail or comes from an existing collaborator; updates should also already be landed upstream unless the TSC grants an exception, and the zlib section neither explains the "-motley" suffix nor names a zlib-specific script.

After updating the OpenSSL sources, regenerate the platform-dependent files in deps/openssl/config/archs/ and the shared generated files in deps/openssl/config/common/. On Linux, run `make -C deps/openssl/config clean` and then `make -C deps/openssl/config`. On other systems, run `make gen-openssl`. Before running make, fix the 32-bit Windows assembler directives in deps/openssl/openssl/crypto/perlasm/x86asm.pl by changing #ifdef/#endif to %ifdef/%endif for nasm. Then stage every change, including added and removed files, with `git add -A deps/openssl/config` and `git add -A deps/openssl/openssl`, and run `git commit` with a message such as "deps: update archs files for openssl-<version>". Node.js C++ unit tests use Google Test and live in `test/cctest` (files named `test_<unit>.cc`); `configure.py` automatically collects every .cc/.h file there into `node_cctest_sources`, which the `cctest` target in node.gyp builds (feature-gated tests go in `node_cctest_openssl_sources`, `node_cctest_quic_sources` or `node_cctest_inspector_sources` instead). To build and run only these tests, run the `cctest` target with `make cctest`. To run a single test case (or several), pass a gtest filter: `make cctest GTEST_FILTER=EnvironmentTest.AtExitWithArgument`. You can also run the built binary directly, which helps when debugging: `out/Release/cctest --gtest_filter=EnvironmentTest.AtExit\*`.

runs.answer: Node.js tests should avoid timers unless the test is specifically testing timers, mainly because timers are a source of flakiness (the doc links to nodejs/testing#27 for the full explanation). If a test really needs a timer, use `common.platformTimeout()` instead of a fixed value. It sets the timeout according to the platform, so `setTimeout(fail, common.platformTimeout(4000))` gives a 4-second timeout on most platforms and a longer one on slower platforms.

Every benchmark file requires `../common.js` and calls `common.createBenchmark(main, configs[, options])`. `main` is the benchmark function that runs the operations and controls the timers. `configs` is an object where each property is an array of possible string or number values, and every combination is run unless specified otherwise. `options` can hold `flags`, `byGroups`, `combinationFilter` and `setup`. `createBenchmark` returns a `bench` object used for timing: inside `main(conf)` you call `bench.start()` after initialization and `bench.end(n)` when done, where `n` is the number of operations performed (usually `conf.n`, which is listed in `configs` so it appears in the report). The script runs twice: the first pass sets up the config combinations without running `main`, and the second runs `main` with the `createBenchmark` flags plus the command-line flags. So code outside `main` runs twice in different processes, and anything more than declarations (including requiring internal modules) belongs inside `main`.

Build two binaries: on `main` run `./configure && make -j4` and `cp ./out/Release/node ./node-main`, then do the same on your branch and copy it to a name like `./node-pr`. Run `node benchmark/compare.js --old ./node-main --new ./node-pr --analyze <benchmark category>`. The tool runs each benchmark many times and does a Welch's t-test inline, with no R needed. Use `--filter <pattern>` to run a single script, `--runs` to set the number of samples (default 30) and `--csv <file>` to keep the raw results. You can also save the CSV and analyze it with `node-benchmark-compare` or `Rscript benchmark/compare.R`. In the output, `improvement` is the new build's relative change and `confidence` stars show significance: `*` means p < 0.05, `**` means 1% risk and `***` means 0.1% risk; with no stars, draw no conclusion. Across many benchmarks (for 20, about one false `*` is normal), the docs suggest a threshold of at least `**`, which may need more `--runs`.

runs.answer: lib/internal/per_context/primordials.js keeps the VM's original JS built-ins so core modules don't later look them up on the global object, which user code can change. Prototype-method primordials such as StringPrototypeSlice wrap the original method in a function that takes `this` as its first argument, so user code that replaces or pollutes a prototype method (for example Array.prototype.push) can't change how core behaves. Primordials are preferred for new code everywhere except node:http, node:http2, node:tls and node:zlib, where performance and readability are judged more important than protection against prototype pollution; replacing existing code with primordials should be done with care. On speed, the docs say some primordials can cause V8 performance regressions that significantly slow a hot code path. The listed ones are ArrayPrototypePush/Pop/Shift/Unshift, FunctionPrototypeBind, FunctionPrototypeCall (when invoking super constructors), FunctionPrototype, SafeArrayIterator, SafeStringIterator, SafePromiseAll/AllSettled/Any/Race, SafePromisePrototypeFinally and ReflectConstruct. StringPrototypeSlice is not on that list, and the docs give no per-method numbers; their general rule is to take extra care and run extensive benchmarks for any PR that changes a hot code path.

runs.answer: Use local symbols created with `Symbol(string)` for internal state. The docs say Node.js often uses them to simulate private fields because they make internals harder to monkey-patch than `_`-prefixed properties, though they are not truly private, since `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols()` can still reach them. The doc's example names the constant with a `k` prefix and uses the same text as the description, e.g. `const kField = Symbol('kField')` and then `this[kField] = ...`; this naming comes from the example, not from a stated rule. `Symbol.for(string)` creates global symbols in a registry shared across the V8 isolate, so two modules can clash on the same key. Use it only when you need a developer-facing interface for behavior customization (metaprogramming), and always prefix the key with `nodejs.`, e.g. `Symbol.for('nodejs.hello')`.

To add a new static error code, append it to the end of `internal/errors.js` with the `E()` helper, for example `E('EXAMPLE_KEY1', 'This is the error value', TypeError);`. The first argument is the identifier. The second is either a message string, which can use `util.format()`-style tags like `%s` and `%d`, or a function that returns a string. The third is the base class the error extends; you can pass more classes, and they become properties such as `EXAMPLE_KEY.RangeError`. You then use it as `const { FOO } = require('internal/errors').codes;` and `throw new FOO(arg)` in place of a plain `new TypeError(...)`. Every new error code you add and use must also be documented in `doc/api/errors.md`, and if `make lint` doesn't detect the new codes there, run `make lint-clean` to clear the markdown lint cache. The docs' examples use generic names like `FOO` and `EXAMPLE_KEY` and give no rule about the `ERR_` prefix.

Prefer returning an error status. The Node.js C++ style guide says to avoid throwing JavaScript errors in C++. A C++ binding method should return to JavaScript the data needed to build the error, and the JS side then creates and throws it using `lib/internal/errors.js`. Argument type checks belong in JavaScript, and the C++ binding should guard against bad arguments only with `CHECK` assertions. If the binding's return value can't signal the failure or carry that data, pass a context object (for example `ctx`) to the binding, set fields such as `code` on it in C++, and have the JS wrapper check `ctx.code` and throw. If you really must throw from C++ (`isolate()->ThrowException()`), do it as close to the return to JavaScript as possible, not inside nested C++ calls. Never use C++ `throw`/`try`/`catch`, because Node.js is built without C++ exception handling.

runs.answer: The docs say the early Fast API limits (no re-entry into JavaScript and no throwing errors directly from fast calls) were removed as of V8 12.6. A fast callback can now access the isolate, allocate `v8::Local` handles on the stack, call into JS and throw. To do any of this it must take a final `v8::FastApiCallbackOptions&` argument (V8 passes the isolate in `options.isolate`). It must also open a `v8::HandleScope` before creating any `v8::Local` handles, so they are scoped and garbage-collected correctly; this includes handles made by functions it calls that don't open their own scope. To throw, it throws a JS error the usual way inside that HandleScope and returns a dummy value that V8 ignores. The docs mention allocation only as stack-allocated `v8::Local` handles, and their one remaining caution is that a function costing far more to run than to call gains little from a fast variant.

runs.answer: According to the docs, the old limits on fast callbacks (no re-entering JavaScript and no throwing errors directly from a fast call) applied to early versions of the Fast API and no longer exist as of V8 12.6. A fast callback may now use the isolate, create `v8::Local` handles on the stack and throw JavaScript errors in the usual way, returning a dummy value afterwards. To do any of this, it must take a final `v8::FastApiCallbackOptions&` argument, which is required "if the callback interacts with the isolate in any way"; V8 passes the isolate in `options.isolate`. The one firm rule is that a fast callback must first open a new `v8::HandleScope` before it creates any `v8::Local` handles. This also applies when it calls helpers that create handles without opening their own scope, and before throwing, because the docs call the scope "mandatory before any operations which create local handles." The docs also warn that a function whose execution cost is far higher than its calling cost is unlikely to benefit from a fast variant.

runs.answer: Valgrind slows execution a lot, so first reduce the problem (here, the http2 stream-cancellation case) to the smallest reproduction you can. Then install Valgrind (for example `apt-get install valgrind`) and run `valgrind node test.js`. When the leak is in the Node.js binary itself rather than in an addon, a release build's stack shows function names (Node exports them with `-rdynamic`) but not the line. So the next step is to check out the Node.js source for that release and build a debug build with `./configure --debug` and then `make -j4`. `make` builds two binaries, and you must run Valgrind with the one in `out/Debug`; the leak records then show the exact source file and line of the allocation (e.g. `inspector_agent.cc:140`), and you read that code to find the fix. The docs only describe this general method and say nothing specific to http2 or stream cancellation.

runs.answer: Node's pull request guide says the first line of the commit message must start with the name of the changed subsystem, then a colon and a short description that begins with an imperative verb (e.g. `net: add localAddress and localPort to Socket`). runs.answer: Yes, if the flag counts as a stable public API: the collaborator guide says backward-incompatible changes to stable public APIs must go through deprecation unless an exception applies (for example, a one-time TSC exception), but experimental or undocumented APIs are usually removed without a deprecation cycle unless people across the ecosystem rely on them. There are three levels: (1) Documentation-Only, a notice in the docs with no functional change and a warning only under --pending-deprecation or NODE_PENDING_DEPRECATION; it can land in a minor release and is not semver-major. (2) Runtime, a warning on first use that becomes an error under --throw-deprecation; this is semver-major. (3) End-of-Life, where the API is outside semver and can be removed at any time; this is also semver-major. A "deprecation cycle" is one major release at a given level: a Documentation-Only deprecation can't become Runtime until the next major, nothing can reach End-of-Life (removal) without a Runtime cycle first, and no deprecation is ever required to move to a later stage. Each deprecation gets a unique, permanent ID whose docs stay even after removal, and PRs that add or change a deprecation level get the notable-change label. The docs frame all of this in terms of "APIs" and never name command-line flags or say whether --jitless is stable or experimental.

runs.answer: The queue lands a PR only if it is author ready, every commit follows the commit message guidelines (or is a valid `fixup!` commit that `--autosquash` handles), a CI run has passed since the last change (only Jenkins CI and GitHub Actions are checked), a collaborator has approved it since the last change, and it targets `main`; PRs against other branches, such as backports, are ignored. The queue also checks a wait time with `@node-core/utils`, counted from when the PR was opened: 48 hours with at least two approvals, seven days with one, and none for correctly approved fast-track PRs. If wait time is the only unmet condition, the queue keeps the label and retries later, so a removed label with a comment means a hard failure. On a hard failure the queue removes `commit-queue`, adds `commit-queue-failed` and posts a comment giving the reason and how to retry; fix the cause, then remove `commit-queue-failed` and add `commit-queue` again. For a PR with several commits, add `commit-queue-squash` to squash them into the first commit, or `commit-queue-rebase` to land them separately, in which case each commit must pass all tests on its own.

runs.answer: Commits merged to `main` reach a release line by being cherry-picked (`git cherry-pick`) onto that line's staging branch, `vN.x-staging` (e.g. `v24.x-staging`), usually by Release Working Group volunteers. A change that is not semver-major ships first in the next Current release and can go into LTS releases after at least two weeks there. If the cherry-pick doesn't apply cleanly or breaks tests, a releaser labels the original PR `backport-requested-vN.x`, meaning someone must open a manual backport PR against `vN.x-staging`; that label is later replaced by `backported-to-vN.x` (once the backport PR merges) or by `dont-land-on-vN.x`. `dont-land-on-v24.x` means the change does not apply to the v24.x line, or that backporting it is more work than it is worth, so it is held back from that branch's releases until the label is removed. Of the related labels, `land-on-vN.x` marks a PR as scheduled for an LTS release, `lts-watch-vN.x` asks the Release WG to consider it, `vN.x` is added automatically to PRs that target `vN.x-staging` instead of `main`, and once a line enters maintenance these labels are no longer needed because only important bug fixes go in.

runs.answer: Commits land on `main` first. Releasers and backporters then cherry-pick them, as appropriate, onto each release line's `vN.x-staging` branch, usually by running `branch-diff vN.x-staging upstream/main`. Staging commits reach the real `vN.x` branch only when a release is being prepared, and only @nodejs/backporters land commits on LTS staging branches. LTS lines also want commits to spend at least two weeks in Current first (the `baking-for-lts` label). A change that applies only to one release line is opened as a PR straight against `vN.x-staging`, and those PRs get the `vN.x` label automatically. `dont-land-on-vN.x` marks a change that does not apply to that line, or one where backporting costs more than it is worth. `branch-diff` leaves out PRs carrying that label, along with `semver-major` and the `backport-requested`/`-blocked`/`-open` and `backported-to-vN.x` labels; reverts and the PRs they revert also get it. If a cherry-pick does not apply cleanly, the original PR gets `backport-requested-vN.x`, and someone opens a manual backport PR against `vN.x-staging` titled `[vN.x backport] <title>`. The label then changes to `backport-open-vN.x` and, after merge, to `backported-to-vN.x`; otherwise it is eventually replaced by `dont-land-on-vN.x`.

runs.answer: Each release line has a `vN.x` branch and a `vN.x-staging` branch. Commits that land on `main` are cherry-picked into the staging branch as appropriate, and staging commits reach `vN.x` only when a release is being prepared. Releasers find the candidate commits with `branch-diff vN.x-staging upstream/main --exclude-label=semver-major,dont-land-on-vN.x,backport-requested-vN.x,backport-blocked-vN.x,backport-open-vN.x,backported-to-vN.x`. For LTS lines they also exclude `baking-for-lts`, because commits must mature in Current for at least two weeks first. If a commit does not cherry-pick cleanly, the original PR is labeled `backport-requested-vN.x` and someone opens a manual backport PR against `vN.x-staging` titled `[vN.x backport] <commit title>`. The original PR's label then moves to `backport-open-vN.x` and then `backported-to-vN.x`. A change that applies only to one line is opened directly against its staging branch and gets the `vN.x` label automatically. `dont-land-on-vN.x` means the change does not apply to that release line, or that backporting it costs more than it is worth, so the cherry-pick list skips it. A `backport-requested` label is eventually replaced by either `dont-land-on` or `backported-to`, and a revert PR and the PR it reverts both get `dont-land-on` labels. Two related labels: `lts-watch-vN.x` asks the Release working group to consider a PR for LTS but promises no action, and releasers use `land-on-vN.x` to mark a PR scheduled for an LTS release.

runs.answer: Once the `vN.x-staging` branch is up to date, generate the proposal with the `create-release-proposal` action (`gh workflow run "Create Release Proposal" -f release-line=N -f release-date=YYYY-MM-DD`) or locally with `git node release -S --prepare x.y.z` (add `--newVersion` for a semver-minor). Either one does every step before step 6, including the version bump, the changelog and the release commit; to do it by hand, branch `vx.y.z-proposal` off `upstream/vN.x-staging`. For the changelog by hand (step 4), run `changelog-maker --group --format=markdown` (add `--filter-release --start-ref <last tag>` if the last tag is not on the branch). Put the entry at the top of `doc/changelogs/CHANGELOG_VN.md`, not the root `CHANGELOG.md`, headed `## YYYY-MM-DD, Version x.y.z (LTS), @releaser`, with a "Notable changes" section (commits labelled `notable-change`/`semver-minor`, e.g. from `branch-diff upstream/vN.x vx.y.z-proposal --require-label=notable-change --plaintext`) and a "Commits" section; then add a bold link at the top of the root `CHANGELOG.md` index and remove the bold from the previous release, run `make format-md`, and replace the `REPLACEME`/`DEP00XX` tags. For the release commit (step 5), commit the `CHANGELOG.md`, `CHANGELOG_VN.md`, `src/node_version.h` and `REPLACEME` changes as the single final commit, with the message `YYYY-MM-DD, Version x.y.z (Release Type)`, then `Notable changes:` with the list in plain text, then `PR-URL: TBD`; after that comes step 6, "Propose release on GitHub". If this is the release that first marks the line as LTS (adding the codename), "LTS Releases" says to check out `vN.x-staging` and run `git node release --prepare --startLTS` as a semver-minor release. That command bumps the minor version, sets the patch to 0 and sets `NODE_VERSION_IS_LTS`=1 and the codename; you also update the changelogs, create the `lts-watch-vN.x` label, and add the codename to nodejs-latest-linker and to the Release repo's README/schedule.json.

For an LTS line, use branch-diff to also exclude the `baking-for-lts` label, and diff against a Current version released at least two weeks before the release date. Put the entry at the top of `doc/changelogs/CHANGELOG_Vx.md`, not the root `CHANGELOG.md`, as `## YYYY-MM-DD, Version x.y.z (LTS), @releaser` with `### Notable changes` (notable-change/semver-minor commits, found with `branch-diff ... --require-label=notable-change`) and `### Commits`. Also add the release to the index table at the top of `CHANGELOG.md` (bold the new release, unbold the previous one), run `make format-md`, and replace the `REPLACEME` tags. The release commit is the final commit and contains the CHANGELOG.md, CHANGELOG_Vx.md, node_version.h and REPLACEME changes, with the message `YYYY-MM-DD, Version x.y.z (Release Type)` / `Notable changes:` (the list in plain text) / `PR-URL: TBD`. Then push the branch to nodejs/node, open a PR against `vN.x` with the changelog in the body (left open at least 24h), and amend the commit with the real PR-URL. If this release is the one that marks the line as LTS (a new codename and a minor bump), the docs say to run `git node release --prepare --startLTS` from the staging branch instead. That command sets NODE_VERSION_IS_LTS=1 and the codename, bumps the minor with patch 0 as a semver-minor release, and updates the changelogs for the Current→LTS move.

runs.answer: Node.js now makes one major release a year. At branch-off in October, about six months before the major, new `vN.x` and `vN.x-staging` branches are forked from `main`, and the semver-major `N.0.0` release ships in April (aimed at the third Tuesday, and it must not slip into May). Between branch-off and the April release, the line ships as Alpha releases. These pick up commits from `main` and, unlike Current and LTS lines, may contain SEMVER-MAJOR changes. They are versioned `vN.0.0-alpha.X.Y.Z`, where X.Y.Z is semver relative to the previous Alpha and the first is `vN.0.0-alpha.0.0.0`. They are labeled "Alpha" in `CHANGELOG_V{N}.md` and published as GitHub pre-releases, and the first Alpha is targeted for the same day the previous line graduates to LTS. The April `N.0.0` release takes the line "out of Alpha": the `NODE_ALPHA_*` macros are removed and the changelog labels change from "Alpha" to "Current". Every semver-major change must land in an Alpha before then, or it goes to the next major line. After that, non-semver-major commits go to the next Current release and can go into LTS releases after at least two weeks in Current, while a semver-major change waits for the next Alpha (up to about 6 months). From Node.js 27, ABI-breaking changes may land during the Alpha and Current phases but are strongly discouraged once a line enters LTS.

runs.answer: A new major release line comes out once a year. It branches off in October, when the `vN.x` and `vN.x-staging` branches are forked from `main`, and the semver-major release ships in April (target: the third Tuesday, and it must not slip into May). Between branch-off and the major release, the line ships as Alpha versions that take commits from `main`. Unlike Current and LTS lines, Alpha releases may contain SEMVER-MAJOR changes, and the first Alpha should come out the same day the previous line graduates to LTS. Alpha versions use the format `vN.0.0-alpha.X.Y.Z`, where X.Y.Z follows semver relative to the previous Alpha and the first is `vN.0.0-alpha.0.0.0`; they are published on GitHub as pre-releases and labeled "Alpha" in the changelog. In April the line is marked "out of Alpha": the `NODE_ALPHA_*` macros are removed and the "Alpha" labels become "Current". Every semver-major change must land in an Alpha first, or it waits for the next major line. Non-semver-major changes go first to the next Current release and can go into LTS after at least two weeks in Current; ABI-breaking changes may land during the Alpha and Current phases but are strongly discouraged once a line enters LTS.

runs.answer: The docs say to build Node.js with GN through V8's node-ci harness. First install depot_tools and add it to PATH; `which gn` should point to depot_tools/gn, and on Windows you also set DEPOT_TOOLS_WIN_TOOLCHAIN=0. Then run `mkdir node_gn && cd node_gn && fetch node` (or `fetch --no-history node`). This puts node-ci at `node_gn/node` and the Node.js source at `node_gn/node/node`, which holds the GN files: `node.gni` for public GN args, plus `*/BUILD.gn` files that only include `*/unofficial.gni`, where the real build rules are. To build, `cd node_gn/node`, run `./tools/gn-gen.py out/Release` to generate ninja files (`--help` lists the options), then run `ninja -C out/Release node`; the binary ends up at `out/Release/node`. Node's CI does not test GN builds and the GN build is not fully working (some tests fail), so you have to check fixes locally, and the docs do not say how to point this workspace at your own branch instead of the latest main.

The GN build files are `node.gni` (public build arguments), `*/BUILD.gn`, which only includes `unofficial.gni`, and `*/unofficial.gni`, which holds the actual build rules. runs.answer: Yes. The 'Building Node.js with Ninja' guide says building with Ninja "can be significantly quicker than using make". Install Ninja using the instructions on ninja-build.org, which the guide marks as Unix only. The guide does not talk about incremental rebuilds as such. The Makefile supports Ninja: run `./configure --ninja` once, then keep using the regular `make` commands. `make` then runs `ninja -C out/Release` internally, links `out/Release/node` to `./node` (`ln -fs out/Release/node node`), and shows `[finished/total]` progress as it builds. Ninja builds run in parallel by default, based on the number of CPUs, and `make -jN` limits the number of jobs; on macOS with GNU Make 3.x, `-jn` doesn't work, so use `make JOBS=n` or upgrade to Make 4.x. For a debug build, run `./configure --ninja --debug && make`. If the binary has a different name (for example `ninja-build` on RHEL7 and below), run `./configure --ninja && NINJA="ninja-build" make`. The `--node-builtin-modules-path "$(pwd)"` option is only for changes limited to the JS layer in `lib/`, so it doesn't apply to C++ work in `src/`.

runs.answer: The PostHog docs say to run tests through `hogli test`, not a bare `pytest` command. To run one test file or directory, use `hogli test <file_or_directory>`, which detects the test type itself (Python, Jest, Playwright, Rust, Go). To run a single test case, use `hogli test path/to/test.py::TestClass::test_method`. You can add `--watch` for watch mode (`hogli test path/to/test.py --watch`), or run `hogli test --changed` to test only changed files. runs.answer: Django serializers are the source of truth for frontend API types: `hogli build:openapi` builds the OpenAPI spec with drf-spectacular, then uses Orval to generate TypeScript into `frontend/src/generated/core/` and `products/{product}/frontend/generated/`. Never hand-edit the generated `api.schemas.ts`, `api.ts` or `api.zod.ts`. Change the serializer and regenerate instead. Run `hogli build:openapi` again after you change serializers or viewsets; a `build:openapi` CI gate enforces this, along with the `prefer-codegen-api` lint and `test_generated_files_are_registered.py`. For the spec to be complete, API views must declare their request/response schemas with `@validated_request` (from `posthog.api.mixins`) or `@extend_schema`, and serializer fields need `help_text`. A ViewSet method that validates manually without `@extend_schema(request=...)` produces an empty schema, and the same spec also generates the MCP tool schemas (the full pipeline is in docs/published/handbook/engineering/type-system.md).

runs.answer: Every tenant-data model must have `team_id` (an FK to `posthog.Team`, or a plain `BigIntegerField` for multi-DB products). This is the main boundary between tenants. The `idor-lookup-without-team` lint and `check-idor-model-coverage.py` enforce it, and new models inherit `TeamScopedRootMixin` (main DB) or `ProductTeamModel` (separate DB) so they are fail-closed. Outside a request (Temporal activities, Celery tasks, management commands), reads go through `Model.objects.for_team(team_id)`; `Model.all_teams.filter(...)` and `objects.unscoped()` are only for genuinely cross-team access and Django internals, and serializers get the team from `self.context["get_team"]()`. `for_team(...).create()` and `.get_or_create()` still need `team_id` passed explicitly, and a model without `team_id` must be org-scoped, user-scoped or instance-global, which only code review checks. For HogQL, the indexed docs have no explicit "every query must be filtered by team" rule: they only say to read `.agents/security.md` before building HogQL strings (it covers injection and least privilege) and to use the `/writing-clickhouse-queries` skill when changing an `execute_hogql_query` or QueryRunner call site, and neither of those is in the index.

runs.answer: PostHog's MCP tools are generated from the same OpenAPI spec as the frontend types, so the backend view first has to declare its request and response schemas. Use `@validated_request` from `posthog.api.mixins` or drf-spectacular's `@extend_schema`. A plain ViewSet method that validates by hand needs `@extend_schema(request=YourSerializer)`, or the generated schema comes out empty. Serializer fields also need `help_text`, because it flows into the MCP tool schemas. The tool itself is set up in the product's YAML config (`products/<product>/mcp/tools.yaml`) and produced by codegen, which is described in the handbook guide `docs/published/handbook/engineering/ai/implementing-mcp-tools.md`. Agents must invoke the `/implementing-mcp-tools` skill whenever they add or change endpoints or `tools.yaml`; the indexed docs point to that skill and guide for the step-by-step YAML and codegen details rather than repeating them.

runs.answer: The build system passes `--cfg bootstrap` whenever it builds with the stage0 compiler, so `cfg(not(bootstrap))` limits code to builds by stage1, and `cfg(bootstrap)` limits it to the stage0 build. The docs say this is used for features that were just stabilized: under stage0 they still need `#![feature(...)]`, but under stage1 they don't. Separately, the build sets `RUSTC_BOOTSTRAP=1` so that `#![feature(...)]` works on the non-nightly beta compiler. By default the stage0 compiler is the recent beta `rustc`, which bootstrap downloads, and it compiles only `src/bootstrap` and `compiler/rustc`, using the precompiled stage0 std rather than the std in the tree. So the stage1 compiler is built with the precompiled stage0 compiler and std, and you need stage2 to get a compiler whose std is freshly built from the tree.

runs.answer: The stage0 compiler is the downloaded recent beta `rustc` with its precompiled std. It is used only to compile `src/bootstrap` and the compiler (`compiler/rustc`). After that, `library`/std is built by the newly built stage1 compiler: `./x build library` builds rustc with the stage0 compiler and stage0 std, then builds `library` with stage1. The build system passes `--cfg bootstrap` when building with stage0, so `#[cfg(bootstrap)]` code is compiled only by the beta compiler. Use `cfg(not(bootstrap))` for features that only the stage1 build should use, because the beta doesn't support them yet. For a feature that was just stabilized, the beta still treats it as unstable, so the stabilization guide says to change `#![feature(XXX)]` in `std` and rustc crates to `#![cfg_attr(bootstrap, feature(XXX))]`. That covers test folders under `library/` and `compiler/` but not the top-level `tests/`. Applying that rule here: if `stdarch_loongarch` was just stabilized, compiler crates that use it still need `#![cfg_attr(bootstrap, feature(stdarch_loongarch))]` because the beta stage0 compiler builds them.

runs.answer: Use compiletest revisions. Put `//@ revisions: foo bar` at the top of the test, and compiletest compiles and tests the file once per revision, passing `--cfg foo`, `--cfg bar` and so on. To give one revision its own flags, write the revision name in brackets after `//@`, as in `//@[foo] compile-flags: -Z verbose-internals`. Error annotations can be limited the same way, as in `//[foo]~ ERROR ...` or `//[foo,bar]~^`. When the revisions produce different compiler output, each revision gets its own expected output file named `<test>.<revision>.stderr` (for example `.mir.stderr` and `.thir.stderr`). Only error patterns and compiler flags are meant to work per revision; "ignore" directives apply to the whole test.

runs.answer: Use the `revisions` directive. Put `//@ revisions: foo bar` at the top of the test, and compiletest compiles and tests the file once per revision, passing `--cfg <name>` each time. Give each revision its own flags with a directive scoped to it, such as `//@[foo] compile-flags: ...`. Scope error annotations the same way, such as `//[foo]~ ERROR ...`, and you can list several revisions with commas, as in `//[foo,bar]~^`. When the revisions produce different output, each one gets its own snapshot named `test-name.revision.stderr` (for example `.mir.stderr` and `.thir.stderr`), which `--bless` generates. Only compiler flags and error patterns are meant to work per revision (the `ignore-*` directives apply to the whole test), and compare modes are a separate mechanism you run by hand with `--compare-mode`.

An error annotation has to match the line where the diagnostic is reported. A plain `//~ ERROR` only matches the line it is written on, so it stops matching once the span moves up a line. Use `//~^ ERROR ...` to point at the line above. Each extra caret moves it up one more line, so `//~^^^^` means four lines above. Other forms: `//~| ERROR` uses the same line as the annotation just before it, which helps when one line has several messages. `//~v` (or `//~vv` and so on) points at lines below. `//~? ERROR` matches a diagnostic that has no line information.

runs.answer: UI-test error annotations are matched to the line where the diagnostic is reported, so a plain `//~ ERROR msg` only matches an error on its own line. To target the line above, use `//~^ ERROR msg`. Each caret moves the target up one line, so `//~^^^^` means four lines above the annotation. `//~| ERROR msg` matches the same line as the annotation just before it, which is handy when one line has several messages. `//~v` (one `v` per line, e.g. `//~vvv`) targets lines below, and `//~?` matches diagnostics with no line info. So when your span moves to the previous line, either move the `//~ ERROR` onto that line or change it to `//~^ ERROR` on the following line.

Regression test for <https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/162109>." Crash tests are the only exception, since they are named only after issue numbers. runs.answer: rustdoc-html tests are Rust source files with HtmlDocCk directives in `//@` comments. compiletest runs them through `src/etc/htmldocck.py`, which checks them against the generated HTML. `//@ has PATH` checks that a file exists, and `//@ has PATH XPATH PATTERN` checks that the text of each element, attribute or text node selected by XPATH in the file at PATH matches the plain string PATTERN, after collapsing runs of whitespace to one space on both sides. `//@ matches PATH XPATH PATTERN` does the same with no whitespace normalization, treating PATTERN as a Python-flavored regex (Unicode-aware, case-sensitive, single-line mode). You select an element with an XPath expression as a shell-style quoted argument, for example `//@ has - '//*[@class="rust item-decl"]//code' 'type Alias = Option<i32>;'`, where `-` reuses the previous PATH (a `#![crate_name = "foo"]` attribute is the usual way to shorten paths). Because HtmlDocCk uses the XPath support in Python's standard library, every XPATH must start with `//`, many XPath features such as functions and axes are unsupported, and negated checks like `//@ !has` are discouraged unless paired with a nearby positive check.

You target elements with an XPath expression, for example `//@ has - '//*[@class="rust item-decl"]//code' 'type Alias = Option<i32>;'`, but because HtmlDocCk uses Python's standard-library XPath, every XPATH must start with `//` and many XPath features (functions, axes) are not supported. Negated forms (`!has`, `!matches`) exist, but the docs discourage them as fragile and say to always pair one with a nearby positive check.

runs.answer: Pass `-Z dump-mir=F`, where F is a filter on function names and pass names. For example, `rustc -Z dump-mir=foo ...` dumps the MIR of every function whose name contains `foo`, both before and after every pass, into the `mir_dump` directory. Each file name shows the function, the pass index, the pass name and whether it is before or after, e.g. `rustc.main.000-000.CleanEndRegions.after.mir`. To compare the two dumps of a single pass, narrow the filter with `&` and `|`: `-Z dump-mir='main & CleanEndRegions'` produces only the `.before.mir` and `.after.mir` files for that pass. Add another field of type `Span` to the struct and put `#[label("message")]` on it, alongside the `#[primary_span]` field. The derive then emits a label at that span. The guide's FieldAlreadyDeclared example does exactly this: `#[label("`{$field_name}` first declared here")] pub prev_span: Span`, which generates `diag.span_label(self.prev_span, "...")`. Fields without an attribute can be used in the message as variables, such as `{$field_name}`. If the other item's span might not exist, make the field `Option<Span>` so the label is only emitted when it is `Some(..)`. A `Vec<Span>` field repeats the label for each element, and `#[note("...")]` on a `Span` field gives a note with a span instead of a label.

runs.answer: Not every suggestion should be applied mechanically. runs.answer: When code or an identifier appears in a diagnostic message or label, it must be surrounded with backticks, e.g. "error: the identifier `foo.bar` is invalid". The reason must be `FutureIncompatibilityReason::EditionError` or `FutureIncompatibilityReason::EditionSemanticsChange`. With an edition-tied reason, `LintStore::register_lints` automatically puts the lint in the matching `rust-20xx-compatibility` group. `cargo fix --edition` passes `--force-warn rust-20xx-compatibility` (and `--cap-lints=allow`), so the lint fires during migration. Add the feature name to the `Symbols {...}` block in `rustc_span/src/symbol.rs` (keep it in alphabetical order). Then declare the gate in the unstable `declare_features` block of `rustc_feature/src/unstable.rs` as `(unstable, $feature_name, "CURRENT_RUSTC_VERSION", Some($tracking_issue_number))`. You can use `None` until a tracking issue exists, and you mark the gate `incomplete` for a lang experiment. Where the feature is used, check `tcx.features().$feature_name()`. If the gate is not set, either keep the old behavior or raise an error, which should generally go through `rustc_session::errors::feature_err` (PR #81015 is the example to follow). New syntax is gated before expansion instead: record the span with `self.psess.gated_spans.gate(sym::my_feature, span)` and deny it in `rustc_ast_passes::feature_gate::check_crate`, usually with `gate_all!()`. Const stability is recursive, so a const-stable fn cannot call `rustc_const_unstable` functions, even indirectly; the guide points to `rustc_const_stable_indirect` and `rustc_allow_const_fn_unstable` for adjusting that check.

Builtin (inert) attributes are parsed during AST lowering by parsers in `rustc_attr_parsing`, which produce a variant of `AttributeKind` in `rustc_attr_ir` (each variant also needs an entry in `encode_cross_crate.rs`). To move validation there, create a struct in `rustc_attr_parsing/attributes/*.rs` (usually empty) and implement one of four traits: `NoArgsAttributeParser` (appears once, no arguments, e.g. `#[no_mangle]`), `SingleAttributeParser` (appears once, with arguments, e.g. `#[inline(...)]`), `CombineAttributeParser` (appears several times, combined into one parsed attribute, e.g. `#[feature(...)]`), or the general `AttributeParser` for attributes that fit none of these (e.g. `#[stable]`/`#[unstable]` combined). Then set the trait's constants (`PATH`, `TEMPLATE` via `template!`, `STABILITY`, `ALLOWED_TARGETS` using `AllowedTargets::AllowList`, `ON_DUPLICATE`, `SAFETY`) and write the parse functions, which get an `AcceptContext` and an `ArgParser`; on bad arguments, emit an error with `cx.adcx().expected_*` and `return None`, or use `cx.expect_*` with `?`. The parser should do every check it can before returning the parsed attribute, it must be registered in `ATTRIBUTE_PARSERS`, and only checks that need more information than the parser has stay as an extra step in `rustc_passes/check_attr.rs`, which runs once the HIR is fully built (code then reads the parsed form with `find_attr!`). The docs give only this general recipe and say nothing specific about `#[doc(keyword)]` or `#[doc(attribute)]`.

runs.answer: rustc tracks hygiene by attaching a context to AST nodes through `Span`, which is just a compact code location plus a `SyntaxContext`; an `Ident` is an interned `Symbol` plus a `Span`, and nodes not produced by a macro have the root context. `ExpnId` is the "macro ID": each macro call gets an integer ID, numbered from 0 in the order the calls are discovered. All three expansion hierarchies (kept in the global `HygieneData` in `rustc_span::hygiene`) start at `ExpnId::root`, which is its own parent. A `SyntaxContext` is an ID for a whole chain of marks in the macro-definition hierarchy. Its `SyntaxContextData` is mostly a cache of filtered views of that chain, with `parent` as the child-to-parent link and `outer_expns` as the individual elements; marks are chained with `SyntaxContext::apply_mark`, so a token with context X that a macro produces gets `X -> macro_id` (built-in macros and proc macros use `SyntaxContext::empty().apply_mark(expn_id)` and count as defined at the root). The last element alone does not determine a chain, so `ExpnId` is not isomorphic to `SyntaxContext`: for `macro m($i: ident) { macro n() { ($i, bar) } }` with `m!(foo)`, `foo` ends with `ROOT -> id(n)` but `bar` ends with `ROOT -> id(m) -> id(n)`.

runs.answer: A `SyntaxContext` is an ID for a whole chain in the "macro definition hierarchy", one of the three expansion hierarchies that make up a crate's hygiene data. That hierarchy tracks when expanding one macro reveals another macro definition. `SyntaxContextData` holds the data for each context, mostly cached results of filtering the chain: `parent` is the child-to-parent link and `outer_expns` are the chain's elements. Each element is an `ExpnId`, the "macro ID" given to every macro call as an integer counting up from 0, and all hierarchies start at `ExpnId::root`. Marks are chained with `SyntaxContext::apply_mark`, so a token with context `X` that a macro outputs gets `X -> macro_id` (e.g. `ROOT -> id(m)`). Built-in macros and proc macros use `SyntaxContext::empty().apply_mark(expn_id)` and count as defined at the root; these contexts are created during expansion while the macro output is merged into the AST. A chain is not determined by its last element, so `ExpnId` is not isomorphic to `SyntaxContext`, and a `Span` is just a compact code location plus a `SyntaxContext`.

runs.answer: Name resolution lives in the rustc_resolve crate, with the bulk in lib.rs and helper or symbol-type-specific logic in other modules (e.g. rustc_resolve::macros, rustc_resolve::late, rustc_resolve::diagnostics), and it runs in two phases. The early phase runs during macro expansion: it builds the module tree and resolves only imports (which need recursive fixed-point resolution) and macro paths (in rustc_resolve::macros, which also reports errors like "not found", "found, but it's unstable" and "expected x, found y"). No other names are resolved at that point. Once the fully expanded AST exists, late resolution (rustc_resolve::late, via Resolver::resolve_crate) walks the tree top-down and resolves every remaining name in the crate, including those in function bodies, using a separate Rib stack per namespace (types, values, macros, plus one for labels); blocks are scanned for items first, each name is resolved only once, and a failed lookup is a compiler error. This late phase also produces diagnostics such as typo suggestions, traits to import and unused-item lints, with import suggestions coming from lookup_import_candidates in rustc_resolve::diagnostics; the guide notes the chapter is incomplete (TODO #16).

runs.answer: The new solver treats canonical cycles as a sign of an infinite proof tree and resolves them by fixpoint iteration. When it hits a cycle, it first returns a provisional result: success (`Yes` with no constraints) if the cycle is coinductive, or `Overflow` if it is inductive. It then re-evaluates the cycle heads until the provisional result matches the result of the latest iteration; after the first iteration, whether the cycle is coinductive or inductive no longer matters. Only auto-trait, `Sized` and `WF` goals currently count as coinductive, and every other cycle is inductive and starts as `Overflow`; also, only the cycle root's result (the root being the deepest goal on the stack involved in any cycle) may go into the global cache. For projections, the future-work section says `normalizes_to` goals must be 'productive' (cyclic `type Assoc = <() as Trait>::Assoc;` would otherwise equal any type), notes this is not relevant to the current solver, and leaves the provisional-cache section and parts of the coinduction chapter as TODOs.

runs.answer: The new solver treats a (canonical) cycle, where a goal depends on itself, as a sign of an infinite proof tree. It handles cycles by iterating to a fixpoint on the cycle heads: the first time a cycle is hit, it returns a provisional result with no constraints. That result is success (`Yes`) if the cycle is coinductive and overflow if it is inductive. It then re-evaluates the head until the provisional result equals the result of that iteration, and after the first iteration it no longer matters whether the cycle was coinductive or inductive. Whether a cycle is inductive or coinductive depends on the goals in it. Currently only auto-trait goals, `Sized` goals and `WF` goals count as coinductive, so other cycles, such as plain trait or `normalizes_to` projection cycles, are inductive and give `Overflow` rather than success. The docs say the plan is to make nearly all goals coinductive, but `normalizes_to` would need to be "productive" (e.g. `type Assoc = <() as Trait>::Assoc;` must not be treated as holding). Also, cycle participants other than the root are not moved to the global cache until the root is finished.

runs.answer: A higher-ranked predicate such as `for<'a> T: Trait<'a>` is wrapped in a `Binder`, which records the variables it introduces (how many, and whether each is a type, const or region, as `BoundVariableKind`). Each use inside is a `RegionKind::Bound`/`TyKind::Bound`/`ConstKind::Bound`, made of a `DebruijnIndex` (which binder, counted outward from the innermost one) and a `BoundVar` (which of that binder's parameters), written `^Debruijn_BoundVar`; rustc ICEs if it builds a binder with escaping bound vars or vars from another binder. Before accessing the inside of a `Binder` you must discharge it by replacing the bound vars, because they mean nothing outside that binder (for example, inferring `T = &'^0 u32` would be nonsensical and probably unsound). Use inference variables (`InferCtxt::instantiate_binder_with_fresh_vars`) when you care about one specific instantiation, such as using a higher-ranked where-clause to prove a bound; use placeholders (`InferCtxt::enter_forall`) to reason about all possible instantiations; and use `liberate_late_bound_regions` (which gives `ReLateParam`s, the `Binder` version of `EarlyBinder::instantiate_identity`) when you are already inside a function's or closure's late-bound binder. The docs never mention `skip_binder` (or `map_bound`/`rebind`), so they do not say when skipping the binder without instantiating it is safe; that part of the question is not answered.

runs.answer: The MIR borrow checker starts at the `mir_borrowck` query in the `rustc_borrowck` crate. It first makes a local copy of the MIR. It then calls `replace_regions_in_mir` to replace every region in that copy with a fresh inference variable, and runs dataflow analyses that work out what data is moved and when. Next, a second type check over the MIR (the MIR type check) collects all the constraints between regions. Region inference comes right after that: it solves those constraints to find each region's value, meaning the points in the control-flow graph where each lifetime must be valid. With those values it computes the "borrows in scope" at each point, then makes a final walk over the MIR that checks each action and reports errors (for example, that a variable is initialized and not mutably borrowed); this walk needs the results of all the earlier steps.

runs.answer: The interpreter's "virtual memory" is the `Memory` type: every global, stack variable and dynamic allocation gets its own `Allocation`, sized exactly to fit. There is no global linear heap. Small locals whose address is never taken are kept as `Operand::Immediate`, purely as an optimization. An `Allocation` is basically a sequence of `u8` holding each byte's value, and it has a globally unique `AllocId`. A `Pointer` is an `AllocId` (a symbolic base address) plus an offset, so pointer arithmetic only changes the offset, never the `AllocId`. When a pointer is stored into an `Allocation`, its offset is written as ordinary bytes and its `AllocId` (the provenance) is kept separately in the `relocation` field; the two are put back together when the pointer is read. The other extra field, `undef_mask`, records which bytes are initialized. `Memory` exists only during evaluation, and any pointers in the final constant are interned into a global const-eval memory in `TyCtxt`.

runs.answer: The interpreter's virtual memory is the `Memory` type. In the simplest model, every global, stack variable and dynamic allocation is an `Allocation`, which is basically a sequence of `u8` byte values plus some extra data, and each one has a globally unique `AllocId`. Small stack variables whose address is never taken are kept as `Operand::Immediate`, which is purely an optimization; a `Scalar` is either a `Raw` integer or a pointer (`Scalar::Ptr`), and an immediate can be uninitialized (`ScalarMaybeUndef::Undef`). A `Pointer` is a pair of an `AllocId`, used as a symbolic base address because the real address is unknown during const eval, and a byte offset. There is no global linear heap, so pointer arithmetic only changes the offset and can never move a pointer into a different allocation. When a pointer is stored into an `Allocation`, its offset is written as ordinary bytes and its `AllocId` (the provenance) is kept out-of-band in the allocation's `relocation` field, then the two are put back together on read; a second field, `undef_mask`, records which bytes are initialized (both field names are as the guide gives them). After evaluation, `Memory` is destroyed and any allocations the result points to are interned into a global const-eval memory in `TyCtxt` (`GlobalAlloc`), which can also hold function (`Instance`) and `Static` entries.

When crate B depends on crate A, A's plain non-generic functions do not appear in B's CGUs, but A's non-generic `#[inline]` functions and all of A's generic instantiations, `#[inline]` or not, land in a single CGU of B that still exists after the post-inlining stage. runs.answer: The monomorphization collector works out which concrete instantiations are needed by following what is reachable from non-generic items, recursively. For example, if `main` calls `banana`, which calls `peach::<u64>`, it yields `[main, banana, peach::<u64>]`, and it also adds things like statics; every collected item gets machine code generated. It runs just before MIR lowering and codegen: `rustc_codegen_ssa::base::codegen_crate` calls the `collect_and_partition_mono_items` query, which requests `optimized_mir` for all reachable functions, collects the mono items, and then splits them into codegen units (CGUs). CGUs are what LLVM processes in parallel and what incremental compilation reuses. For better incremental builds, the partitioner makes two CGUs per source-level module, one for stable non-generic code and one for volatile monomorphized instances. For an upstream crate A used by crate B, a non-generic function from A appears in no CGU of B, a non-generic `#[inline]` function appears in a single CGU of B, and all monomorphizations of generic functions from A (inline or not) go into a single CGU of B that survives post-inlining. The guide does not give the finer rules, such as how roots are chosen, whether an item can be instantiated, or export and linkage. It points to the `rustc_monomorphize::collector` and `rustc_monomorphize::partitioning` rustdocs for those, and to `tests/codegen-units` (`-Zprint-mono-items` with `//~ MONO_ITEM name @@ cgu[Linkage]` annotations) for testing the collector and the partitioning.

runs.answer: `rustc_codegen_ssa` defines an abstract interface that every backend (LLVM, Cranelift and GCC) implements. It holds the trait definitions under `rustc_codegen_ssa/traits` (such as `BuilderMethods`, `CodegenMethods`, `CodegenBackend` and `ExtraBackendMethods`) and the backend-agnostic code that is generic over them, such as the MIR lowering in `mir/` and the codegen driving in `base.rs`. Backend-specific code, such as LLVM's FFI and most of its `debuginfo`, stays in the backend crate, for example `rustc_codegen_llvm`. The split was made by replacing LLVM-specific types with generics (`Value`, `BasicBlock`, `Type`) and wrapping every function that calls the LLVM FFI in these traits. Each backend defines its own `CodegenCx` (one codegen unit) and `Builder` (one basic block) structs that implement the traits, plus a top-level struct implementing `ExtraBackendMethods`/`CodegenBackend` (for LLVM, the empty `LlvmCodegenBackend`); agnostic code is written as `fn codegen_instance<'a, 'tcx, Bx: BuilderMethods<'a, 'tcx>>(cx: &'a Bx::CodegenCx, ...)`, using only compile-time generics and no trait objects. The doc warns that the traits' API closely mirrors LLVM's and may need to change to give other backends more flexibility. A search excerpt from the Code generation chapter also says `rustc_codegen_ssa` still contains a fair amount of LLVM-specific code.

runs.answer: For red-green marking, the query engine computes a 128-bit `Fingerprint` of each new query result. It compares that against the previous session's fingerprint, which is stored with the dependency graph, so the old result never has to be loaded from disk or cached. That comparison only works if hashing is done "in a stable way": anything that can change between sessions, such as a `DefId`, is hashed through its stable equivalent (its `DefPath`/`DefPathHash`), and the guide says this is the whole purpose of the stable-hashing infrastructure, which it calls `StableHash`, so that fingerprints from two different sessions stay comparable. A `DefId` is a numeric ID that depends on the source being compiled, so adding a function in the middle of a file can change other items' IDs, while a path-based `DefPath` like `std::collections::HashMap` is unaffected by unrelated changes. The guide never mentions std's `Hash` impl by name, so that part is an inference: hashing a value's in-memory form, raw IDs included, gives fingerprints that depend on the session and cannot be compared across sessions (the guide also calls for a high-quality 128-bit hash so collisions are negligible).

runs.answer: For red-green marking, the compiler must check whether a query result differs from the previous session's without loading the old result from disk, so it computes a 128-bit hash of each new result, its `Fingerprint`, stores it with the dependency graph, and compares old and new fingerprints. That hashing has to be done "in a stable way": anything that can change between compilation sessions, such as a `DefId`, must be hashed through its stable equivalent, such as the `DefPath`/`DefPathHash`, and "that's what the whole `StableHash` infrastructure is for". Only then are fingerprints from two different sessions comparable. A `DefId` is only a numeric ID, and after a source edit like adding a function there is no guarantee anything keeps the same ID, so hashing the raw in-memory value gives session-dependent fingerprints. runs.answer: The rustc-dev-guide says that `modified: src/tools/cargo (new commits)` in `git status` is a change to the submodule, not to any files, and that running `git submodule update` gets rid of it. The guide describes this after `git pull` rather than after switching branches, but the symptom is the same. If `git status` shows `(new commits, modified content)` and `git submodule update` fails, run `git submodule foreach git reset --hard`, then run `git submodule update` again. Don't commit the submodule change with `git add .` (running `x` also updates submodules). If you already committed it by accident, find the commit with `git log --stat -n1 src/tools/cargo`, then run `git checkout <my-commit>~ src/tools/cargo` and `git commit --fixup <my-commit>`, and squash with `git rebase --autosquash -i upstream/main`.

runs.answer: A `.wd-test` test is a Bazel `wd_test()` target. To run one, pass its target to Bazel, e.g. `bazel test //src/workerd/api/tests:encoding-test@`. You can also use `just test //src/workerd/api/tests:encoding-test@`, or `just stream-test <target>` to stream the output while debugging. The `@` suffix is required because the macro generates three variants: `name@` (the default, oldest compat date 2000-01-01), `name@all-compat-flags` (newest compat date, all flags enabled) and `name@all-autogates` (all autogates on, oldest compat date). So you write `//src/workerd/io:io-gate-test@`, not `//src/workerd/io:io-gate-test`. To find the target name, look for the `wd_test()` rule in the `BUILD.bazel` file next to the test, or list a package's targets with `bazel query //src/workerd/api/tests:all`. If `cloudflared access token -app=https://bazelflare-workerd.runtime-playground.workers.dev` prints a token, add `--config=bazelflare` for remote execution; otherwise run locally.

runs.answer: In a .wd-test file, which is a Cap'n Proto Workerd.Config, you turn a flag on by adding its name to the `compatibilityFlags` list in the test worker's definition, next to `compatibilityDate`. For example: `worker = (modules = [(name = "worker", esModule = embed "my-test.js")], compatibilityDate = "2024-01-01", compatibilityFlags = ["nodejs_compat"])`. The build macros also run every test in several variants. The default `name@` variant uses the oldest compat date (2000-01-01), and `name@all-compat-flags` uses the newest date (2999-12-31) with all flags on. So a flag you don't list explicitly will only be on in the `@all-compat-flags` variant.

runs.answer: Every test target automatically gets a `name@all-autogates` variant, which runs with all autogates enabled and the oldest compat date (2000-01-01). To run with all autogates on, target that variant with `just test` or `bazel test`, for example `just test //src/workerd/io:io-gate-test@all-autogates`. The `@` suffix is required, and you can find target names in the directory's `BUILD.bazel` or with `bazel query //pkg:all`. Use `just stream-test <target>` if you want to stream the output. runs.answer: Format your changes with `just format` (or `just f`). It runs clang-format along with prettier, ruff, buildifier and rustfmt. Use `just format <path>...` to format specific files, or `just format-head` for files changed since `HEAD~`. Run clang-tidy on a Bazel target with `just clang-tidy <target>` (e.g. `just clang-tidy //src/rust/jsg:ffi`); the project's custom checks are in `//tools/clang-tidy:workerd-lint`, and `build/AGENTS.md` has more detail. There is a pre-commit hook at `githooks/pre-commit`, which you turn on with `git config core.hooksPath githooks`. It blocks `KJ_DBG` in staged code and runs a format check (see `docs/development.md`), but the docs don't say it runs clang-tidy, so run that yourself.

runs.answer: According to the docs, an autogate (src/workerd/util/autogate.*) is per-process, config-driven and temporary. It is meant for risky rollouts that need conditional activation, and it allows a gradual rollout with a fast rollback. A compatibility flag (src/workerd/io/compatibility-date.capnp) is per-worker, date-driven and permanent, and it must be documented before its enable date. So an autogate fits a risky change whose rollout you want to switch on or off by config for a while. It is not enough on its own when the change alters what existing Workers see: workerd promises that deployed behavior won't change, and compat-date flags are how behavior changes are introduced. Autogates do not preserve existing Workers' API surface, and compatibility breakage may not show up in runtime metrics or may only be reported late by customers, so a quiet rollout does not prove the change is safe. For those changes, use a compatibility flag or explicitly accept the risk, and record that decision in the commit message.

runs.answer: The docs tell the two apart by scope and lifetime. Autogates (`src/workerd/util/autogate.*`) are per-process, config-driven and temporary, and they are meant "for risky rollouts with conditional activation", meaning gradual rollout with fast rollback. Compatibility flags (`src/workerd/io/compatibility-date.capnp`) are per-worker, date-driven and permanent. They are how the project changes behavior, because deployed features cannot be removed or changed. The docs warn that autogates "do not preserve existing Workers' API surface", and that compatibility failures may not show in runtime metrics or may be reported late by customers, so a quiet autogate rollout alone does not prove a change is safe. So a change that existing Workers could notice needs a compatibility flag; for additions to the API surface, the commit message can instead explicitly accept the risk. An autogate fits a temporary, conditionally activated rollout of a risky change, not a way to keep compatibility.

Add the new flag as an entry in src/workerd/io/compatibility-date.capnp (about 1400 lines). Annotations on each entry set the flag names and the enable date, and this file is how the project adds behavior changes without breaking Workers that are already deployed. Compatibility flags apply per worker, are driven by date, and are permanent, and a flag MUST be documented before its enable date. The docs only partly answer the question: they say annotations in that file set the flag names, but they give neither the annotation syntax nor a naming rule for the opposite disable flag.

After that, make sure all tests pass and check the build for new deprecations, flagging them for users if necessary; also find every standard API the update newly enables by default and record its disposition in the commit message (a compatibility flag or explicitly accepting the risk), negating a V8 flag in src/workerd/jsg/setup.c++ rather than deleting it to turn a default off (e.g. --nojs-float16array).
